items.abstract: Abnormal mitochondrial respiratory chain (MRC) activity is a pivotal driver in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, the molecular mechanisms linking it to immune phenotypes and disease progression remain unclear. This study aims to systematically determine core biomarkers of MRC dysfunction in SLE and explore their potential pathogenic mechanisms through multi-scale transcriptomic analysis. Five bulk transcriptomic series from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were integrated to screen for differentially expressed genes linked to MRC abnormalities. Three machine learning algorithms and SHAP analysis were applied to identify core signature genes. Leveraging these markers, a diagnostic model was developed, along with constructing molecular interaction and regulatory networks. We elucidated the biological functions through functional enrichment, immune infiltration analyzes, and correlation analysis with key therapeutic targets. Furthermore, we integrated three single-cell datasets and applied Seurat clustering, pseudotime analysis, and CellChat to characterize the expression patterns, differentiation trajectories, and interaction networks of core genes within specific cell subpopulations. Our results identified 18 biomarkers, with SCO2 emerging as the primary core gene. The diagnostic model achieved high discriminatory accuracy. Multi-dimensional functional analyzes uncovered a potential role for SCO2 bridging mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction with antiviral innate immune activation. Single-cell analysis localized SCO2 overexpression primarily to monocytes and dendritic cells, showing a downregulation trajectory during myeloid differentiation. We found that SCO2 + myeloid cells exhibit altered interaction networks within the immune microenvironment, characterized by enriched MHC-I/II and MIF signaling. In conclusion, SCO2 is a critical biomarker of MRC activity in SLE, reflecting the mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming that drives immune dysregulation.

items.abstract: Abstract Interfacial contact area between contiguous grains governs macroscopic elastic moduli, stress transmission chains, effective thermal and electrical conductivity, and solid-state diffusion rates in three-dimensional (3D) granular media. Standard characterization of X-ray micro-computed tomography (µCT) volumes relies on 3D Euclidean distance transform seeding and marker-controlled watershed segmentation followed by polygonal surface extraction via the Marching-Cubes algorithm (Lorensen & Cline, 1987). However, Cartesian voxelization introduces severe staircase terracing along curved inter-particle boundaries, inflating surface area measurements by 40% to 80%, while local mesh triangulation scales poorly to assemblies containing thousands of grains. Conducted under the supervision of Prof. Mayank Goswami , this study establishes a comparative benchmark of four data-driven surrogate architectures—an interpretable Random Forest ensemble, a 4-block 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D CNN) operating on 48 3 binary dual-particle patches, a 3-layer bidirectional GraphSAGE Graph Neural Network (GNN) operating on the global contact graph G = (V, E) , and a multimodal Hybrid GNN + CNN fusion architecture—across 250 synthetic 3D granular phantoms (50,800 particles and 48,750 contact interfaces). Across 38 held-out test specimens (7,466 contact interfaces), we evaluate models under both DEM-coupled (known sphere geometry) and blind tomographic (voxel-only, zero metadata) operating regimes. When coupled with exact inter-particle distance and radius attributes, the 3-layer bidirectional GraphSAGE network achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.158 vx 2 , a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.217 vx 2 , a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.91% , and R 2 = 0.99999 at an inference latency of 2.89 ms per phantom , while the Random Forest baseline achieves R 2 = 0.99992 and MAE = 0.409 vx 2 . Crucially, an explicit feature-circularity ablation study demonstrates that removing pairwise distance and overlap features collapses tabular/graph accuracy to R 2 = 0.4387 (MAE = 44.68 vx 2 ), proving that inter-centroid geometry is physically indispensable; however, estimating these quantities 100% blindly from watershed-segmented voxels via principal inertia axes ( R̂ i = L maj,i /2, MAE = 0.048 vx) restores R 2 = 0.9959 (MAE = 3.35 vx 2 ) without ground-truth metadata. Furthermore, the purely image-based 4-block 3D CNN —which requires zero tabular or metadata inputs—achieves R 2 = 0.99788 and MAE = 2.434 vx 2 (166.23 ms/phantom), outperforming classical Marching-Cubes surface meshing (MAE = 42.750 vx 2 , MAPE = 72.24%, R 2 = 0.50471, 3,555.60 ms/phantom) by 17.6× in accuracy and 21.4× in speed. Scaling experiments up to N = 2,000 particles, overlap-depth stratification, per-particle contact area aggregation ( n = 6,879 active test grains), and domain adaptation to mildly non-spherical superellipsoids (3D CNN R 2 = 0.9979, MAE = 2.50 vx 2 ) establish practical guidelines, methodological limitations, and ethical safeguards for deploying AI surrogates in granular mechanics.

items.abstract: Abstract The spatial resolution of a computed tomography (CT) scan, summarised by the frequency at which the modulation transfer function falls to one half (MTF50), depends jointly on focal-spot size, geometric magnification, detector blur and reconstruction voxel size. We built a simulation pipeline that scans an analytic slanted-edge and bar-pattern phantom at 400 acquisition settings and measures the ground-truth MTF with the edge-spread-function method and used it to train two kinds of fast estimators. A Gaussian-process surrogate predicts MTF50 from the four settings with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.106 lp/mm and R 2 = 0.983 on held-out settings, compared with 1.285 lp/mm for the classical quadrature blur formula and 0.293 lp/mm for a calibrated version of it, about 2,000 times faster than a single simulation. Adding physics-derived blur features improved every model and kept errors low in several extrapolation scenarios in which raw-feature models failed. A small residual convolutional network that sees only a 64 × 64 image patch reached 0.121 lp/mm per setting, close to the surrogate, but its error rose to 0.60 lp/mm on unseen generic phantoms, exposing a clear out-of-distribution limit. Within the studied ranges, magnification and detector blur were the most influential settings. Code, data and trained models are released.

items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Accurate preoperative prediction of pathological complete response (pCR) following neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is essential for individualized treatment decision-making in patients with breast cancer. This study aimed to develop a multimodal fusion model integrating conventional radiomics, two-dimensional (2D) deep learning features, and clinical risk factors based on the pre-treatment third-phase images of dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI), and to validate its efficacy for predicting pCR in an independent institutional cohort. Methods This retrospective multicenter study enrolled 372 women with breast cancer who received NAC across two centers. The 245 patients from Center 1 constituted the model development cohort and were stratified by pCR status and randomly split at a 7:3 ratio into a training set (n = 171) and an internal validation set (n = 74), whereas the 127 patients from Center 2 served as an independent external test set. A radiologist manually delineated the tumor region of interest on the third contrast-enhanced phase of DCE-MRI, and all delineations were reviewed by a senior radiologist. A total of 1,197 radiomic features were extracted using PyRadiomics; after Spearman correlation-based redundancy removal and dimensionality reduction with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, 10 features were retained to construct the radiomics model. Six ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural networks were compared, and MobileNet V2 was selected to build the 2D deep learning model. After dimensionality reduction by principal component analysis, the deep features were early-fused with the radiomic features to develop a deep learning radiomics (DLR) model. Independent clinical predictors of pCR were identified using univariate and multivariate logistic regression and used to construct a clinical model. The predicted probability of the DLR model was further fused with the independent clinical factors using logistic regression to build the combined model, which was presented as a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, calibration curves, decision curve analysis, the DeLong test, the integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and the net reclassification improvement (NRI). Interpretability analyses were conducted using SHAP and Grad-CAM. Results The pCR rate of the entire cohort was 14.2% (53/372), with rates of 17.0%, 21.6%, and 6.3% in the training, internal validation, and external test sets, respectively. Multivariate logistic regression identified ER status (adjusted OR = 0.119, P < 0.001), HER-2 status (adjusted OR = 4.870, P = 0.003), and maximum tumor diameter (adjusted OR = 0.742, P = 0.041) as independent predictors of pCR. In the independent external test set, the combined model achieved the best overall discriminative performance, with an AUC of 0.933 (95% CI: 0.879–0.987), accuracy of 0.843, sensitivity of 1.000, specificity of 0.832, and negative predictive value of 1.000, outperforming the clinical model (AUC = 0.925), the deep learning model (0.825), the DLR model (0.745), and the radiomics model (0.559); its AUC was significantly higher than those of the radiomics model (P = 0.0007) and the DLR model (P = 0.014). The deep learning model showed the smallest cross-center performance degradation (ΔAUC = 0.033), markedly smaller than that of the conventional radiomics model (ΔAUC = 0.278). Relative to the four single-modality models, the combined model yielded positive IDI (0.208–0.482, all P < 0.05) and NRI (0.216–0.683) values, good calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow test, P = 0.069), and a higher net clinical benefit on decision curve analysis. SHAP and Grad-CAM analyses consistently demonstrated that model decisions focused on intratumoral enhancement heterogeneity and peritumoral regions, with the most contributory features derived from both radiomics and deep learning, indicating complementarity between the two sources of information. Conclusions The multimodal fusion nomogram integrating independent clinical predictors, conventional radiomic features, and 2D deep learning features can accurately and robustly predict pCR after NAC in breast cancer before surgery, with favorable cross-center generalizability and interpretability. It may serve as a noninvasive quantitative tool for evaluating NAC response and supporting individualized treatment decision-making.

items.abstract: Abstract Background: Genetic frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is characterized by substantial clinical and neuroanatomical heterogeneity, making prediction of symptom onset challenging. We evaluated whether deep learning-derived MRI biomarkers could be combined with non-imaging biomarkers in an interpretable framework for diagnosis and phenoconversion prediction in genetic FTD. Methods: We evaluated Multi-ICNN, a multimodal extension of the Interpretable Convolutional Neural Network, using data from the FTD Risk Cohort. Imaging biomarkers derived from T1-weighted MRI were combined with demographic, genetic, and neuropsychological biomarkers in an additive prediction model. We evaluated classification of symptomatic mutation carriers versus genetically confirmed non-carriers and phenoconversion prediction within 2- and 5-year time horizons. Biomarker contributions were examined at the group and participant levels. Results: For diagnosis, Multi-ICNN achieved the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.953, numerically outperforming the single-modality models. For phenoconversion prediction, the deep learning-based models outperformed the conventional volumetric and non-imaging models. The imaging-only ICNN achieved the highest mean AUCs of 0.798 and 0.780 for the 2- and 5-year horizons, respectively. Adding non-imaging biomarkers did not further improve ICNN performance. Neuropsychological measures contributed most strongly to diagnosis, whereas imaging-derived biomarkers dominated phenoconversion prediction, particularly biomarkers involving frontal and temporal regions. The additive model also provided participant-specific biomarker contributions. Conclusions: Interpretable deep learning-derived MRI biomarkers showed promise for phenoconversion prediction in genetic FTD, while the value of multimodal integration depended on the clinical task. The main limitations were the modest sample size and lack of external validation, reflecting the rarity of genetic FTD and the limited availability of comparable longitudinal cohorts.

items.abstract: Background: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a devastating chronic lung disease with an incompletely understood course. Limited quantitative tools complicate consistent patient assessment, and visual evaluation of radiological progression varies between observers. This study aimed to assess baseline and one-year CT scans using artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted 3D quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT), integrating radiological changes with clinical findings to objectively characterize disease progression and examine its association with prognosis. Methods: In this retrospective cohort of 83 patients with IPF, we evaluated patients using an AI-assisted quantitative CT framework for prognostic assessment. Whole-lung segmentation was performed using a pretrained deep learning model (LungMask), followed by semi-automated segmentation of fibrotic abnormalities with radiologist-guided refinement. Quantitative imaging biomarkers, including honeycombing volume, non-honeycomb fibrotic lung volume, preserved lung volume, and the pathological lung volume-to-total lung volume ratio, were derived from 3D QCT analysis. Baseline and one-year measurements and their changes were evaluated in relation to mortality, pulmonary function test, gender, age, physiology score (GAP) index, and composite physiologic index (CPI). Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test, paired comparisons using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and correlations using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 27.0. Results: A total of 83 patients with IPF were included in the study (mean age: 64.1 ± 8.5 years; 69.9% male). First-year mortality was 14.5% (n = 12), and overall mortality was 37.3% (n = 31) over a median follow-up of 48 months. Compared with the survival group, the mortality group had greater baseline non-honeycomb fibrotic lung volume (1002.2 ml ± 532.3 vs. 628.4 ± 460.2), a higher pathological-to-total lung volume ratio, comprising honeycomb and non-honeycomb fibrosis (0.34 ± 0.16 vs. 0.18 ± 0.15), and lower preserved lung volume (2317.9 ± 961.4 vs. 3531.6 ± 1579.2; all p < 0.001). Over one year, honeycomb and non-honeycomb fibrotic lung volume ratios increased, while the preserved lung volume ratio decreased in both groups (all p < 0.05). Patients with a 10% forced vital capacity (FVC) decline had a greater increase in the non-honeycomb fibrotic-to-total lung volume ratio (0.08 ± 0.10 vs. 0.02 ± 0.20; p = 0.044). The baseline pathological-to-total lung volume ratio correlated with baseline GAP (r = 0.343, p = 0.002), baseline CPI (r = 0.431, p < 0.001), and one-year CPI (r = 0.560, p < 0.001). One-year QCT changes did not differ significantly between the mortality and survival groups. Conclusion: 3D semi-automated, AI-assisted QCT provided an objective assessment of radiological progression in IPF. Greater baseline fibrotic involvement and lower preserved lung volume were associated with mortality, and quantitative imaging measures correlated with GAP and CPI. Although one-year QCT changes did not differ by mortality status, increased non-honeycomb fibrotic involvement was associated with FVC decline. These findings support QCT as a complementary tool for assessing disease extent and progression alongside functional and prognostic indices.

items.abstract: Management of pulmonary nodules detected on computed tomography requires assessment of malignancy risk, treatment suitability and the benefits and harms of available options. This narrative review examines clinical decision-making and continuity of care for screening-detected and incidental nodules. Core searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library covered English-language literature from 2010 through August 2026, supplemented by targeted searches and citation tracing. Evidence was selectively synthesized around management decisions. Nodule type, prior imaging and consistent measurement methods guide risk assessment and surveillance. Surveillance intervals and intervention criteria remain specific to the detection setting, the nodule type and the applicable management framework. Further testing is appropriate when its results could change a feasible management plan; negative or nondiagnostic results require interpretation in light of residual malignancy risk. Treatment selection should balance expected benefit against procedural harm and overtreatment, considering cardiopulmonary reserve, frailty, comorbidity, competing mortality risks and patient preferences. Within the reviewed literature, patient-outcome benefit from artificial intelligence has not been established. Continuity of care requires completion of planned actions, review and communication of results, and clear responsibility for subsequent follow-up. Risk-informed decisions should be linked to reliable follow-up, with reassessment as imaging findings or patient circumstances change.

items.abstract: Introduction Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for chronic total occlusions (CTO) remains technically challenging, with lower technical success than non-CTO PCI. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) may improve procedural and stent-related outcomes by supporting procedural planning, lesion crossing, and stent optimization. Areas covered A literature search of PubMed, Google scholar, identified randomized trials, registries, observational studies, meta-analyses, and consensus documents on CCTA and IVUS in CTO PCI. CCTA enables three-dimensional assessment of cap morphology, occlusion length, tortuosity, calcification, and distal vessel quality, refining complexity assessment and strategy selection. IVUS provides real-time guidance for proximal cap identification, guidewire position, reentry techniques, vessel sizing, and stent optimization. Artificial intelligence and image co-registration are also discussed. Expert opinion CCTA and IVUS provide complementary information across the stages of CTO PCI. Selective preprocedural CCTA may be most valuable in anatomically complex lesions, whereas IVUS supports lesion crossing and should be strongly considered for stent optimization. Wider adoption will depend on workflow integration, operator training, automated image analysis, and prospective validation of imaging-guided strategies.

items.abstract: BackgroundA brain tumor is a medical pathology, whereas biomedical imaging is a key element used to visualize the condition. Brain tumor classification is an essential imaging task for early pinpointing and treatment. Accurate and timely tumor characterization supports appropriate treatment planning, prognosis assessment and better patient outcomes.ObjectiveThis paper aims to develop an efficient hybrid deep learning model for early detection of brain tumors from MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) images.MethodsTo classify tumors, this work proposes a hybrid EfficientNet B7 and Inception V4 (ENETV4) network. The Inception network interprets spatial features for improving classification accuracy, while the EfficientNet B7 framework increases the computational efficiency to maintain high feature extraction ability. A unified feature is created by concatenating the retrieved features from the two models. To improve classification performance, a Figshare dataset comprising glioma, meningioma and pituitary tumor MRI images was used. Optimized hyperparameters enhanced generalization across the 70:20:10 train-test-validation split of the multi-sequence MRI dataset.ResultsThe proposed hybrid ENETV4 networks achieved 98.53% accuracy using an independent dataset, outperforming existing methods when evaluated on the dataset. These results accurately differentiate various kinds of tumors. This paper compares the hybrid ENETV4 model with the traditional models, reaffirming that the hybrid ENETV4 method enables effective classification of brain tumors from medical images, helping clinicians select suitable treatment strategies.ConclusionThe proposed hybrid methods provide accurate tumor classification in an early stage, supporting timely clinical decisions and treatment planning.

items.abstract: BackgroundPhoton-counting computed tomography (PCCT) provides finely sampled morphological images and energy-resolved products that may alter the behavior of artificial-intelligence models developed for conventional CT.ObjectiveThis review synthesizes downstream AI applications in PCCT and determines which study designs support claims of feasibility, transfer, spatial or spectral contribution, scanner advantage, and clinical utility.MethodsA structured narrative search identified original studies evaluating segmentation, detection, classification and characterization, and automated quantification on reconstructed PCCT images. Each analytical configuration was coded by task, effective input, model provenance, development or adaptation strategy, reference standard, comparator, testing independence, and evidence maturity.ResultsTechnical feasibility has been demonstrated across all four tasks. Established conventional-domain models often retained useful local performance on PCCT, while PCCT-native studies explored virtual monoenergetic images, threshold or energy-bin images, material maps, and multienergy feature spaces. However, small cohorts, repeated non-independent observations, incomplete external testing, limited matched PCCT-EID comparisons, and scarce spatial or spectral ablations restrict causal attribution. Prospective workflow evidence remains uncommon.ConclusionsPCCT creates important opportunities for AI-enabled image analysis, but availability of high-resolution or energy-resolved information does not establish its contribution to performance. Claims should be aligned with the comparator, ablation, reference standard, and validation design required to support them.

items.abstract: Objectives To develop deep learning super-resolution (SR) models for enhancing cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). Methods Seventy CBCT volumes (75 µm voxel size) served as references. Paired low-resolution (LR) volumes (300 µm) were simulated using physics-based degradation. Four architectures were each trained with three loss configurations (L1; L1+edge; L1+edge+perceptual): Swin Transformer for Image Restoration (SwinIR), Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT), Hybrid Multi-Axis Aggregation Network (HMA-Net), and Dense-Residual-Connected Transformer (DRCT). Performance was assessed with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and deep image structure and texture similarity (DISTS). Three dentists ranked the 12 configurations in 28 sets using blinded forced-choice pairwise comparisons. Correlations of metrics and expert ranks were assessed using Spearman correlation. Results All configurations outperformed LR input and bicubic interpolation on every metric (p < 0.05). HMA-Net trained with L1+edge+perceptual loss performed best on LPIPS (0.216) and DISTS (0.186). HAT with L1 loss achieved the highest PSNR (28.79 dB) and SSIM (0.820). Experts ranked DRCT and HAT with L1 loss, and DRCT with L1+edge loss, as the best configurations (p < 0.001 versus others). Expert rank correlated moderately only with PSNR (rho = -0.65) and SSIM (rho = -0.60; both p < 0.05). Conclusions Transformer-based SR improved the perceived quality of clinical CBCT images. HAT and DRCT trained with L1 pixel loss alone, and DRCT trained with L1 and edge loss, demonstrated superior performance. Advances in knowledge Transformer-based super-resolution improved expert-perceived detail of simulated low-resolution in vivo CBCT scans without additional radiation dose, supporting further validation on directly acquired low-resolution scans.

items.abstract: Objective. To eliminate the reliance on large-scale external training datasets and achieve high-precision alignment for complex brain structures by overcoming the prevalent challenges of data scarcity and domain shifts in current deep learning-based registration methods. Approach. We propose a novel Instance-Specific Deep Brain Registration Framework that independently trains a dedicated model for each specific image pair. By reconceptualizing a single image pair as an internal dataset generator, we introduce a Multi-Scale Random Patch Learning strategy to construct a diverse local-to-global sample space. Architecturally, we design a Context-Aware Flow Predictor integrated with a Recurrent Context Transfer mechanism within a coarse-to-fine paradigm. Furthermore, a Topology-Aware Adaptive Optimization strategy is incorporated during the inference phase. By dynamically tracking the local spatial folding status, it adaptively adjusts spatial regularization to effectively suppress topological distortions while maximizing voxel-level accuracy. Main results. Extensive experiments on mono-modal, multi-modal, and pathological brain MRI datasets demonstrate that our method can handle large anatomical deformations without relying on external training datasets. It achieves highly competitive registration performance compared to mainstream population-based and implicit neural representation methods. Crucially, it balances this alignment precision with effective numerical topology preservation. Significance. This framework challenges the traditional population-based learning paradigm, offering a highly flexible, robust, and promising solution for practical neuroimage analysis, particularly in clinical scenarios characterized by extreme data scarcity and complex cross-modality variations.

items.abstract: Objective This study aimed to rationally design, screen, and experimentally validate novel immunoglobulin domain antibodies (IgDAbs) targeting the site II epitope of the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion (F) protein using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) driven tools. Method A generative AI tool was employed to generate 250 novel IgDAb sequences optimized for RSV-F site II binding. Candidates were screened computationally using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations to select hit candidates. The selected IgDAbs were cloned and produced using an E. coli expression system. Purified IgDAbs were characterized for target specificity via ELISA and evaluated for functional viral inhibition using in vitro microneutralization assay against RSV A2 (long strain). Result Computational screening narrowed the library to 05 structurally compatible hit IgDAb with predicted binding affinity. ELISA confirmed specific binding of purified IgDAbs to the RSV-F protein. In vitro microneutralization assays demonstrated neutralization of RSV A2 (long strain), with two 'lead' IgDAbs showing EC 50 of 1.3 µg/mL and 3.5 µg/mL. Conclusion Combining generative AI sequence generation with an integrated in silico and in vitro screening cascade enables the rapid, cost-effective discovery of neutralizing nanobodies against RSV, offering a viable alternative to resource-intensive traditional antibody discovery workflows.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based protein structure prediction provides new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery, especially for targets lacking experimental structures. Determining whether AlphaFold2- and AlphaFold3-derived models can reliably support structure-based virtual screening remains a critical issue. In this study, we systematically evaluated the applicability of AlphaFold2- and AlphaFold3-derived models for structure-based virtual screening and assessed the performance of different VS pipeline configurations that integrate AlphaFold models with diverse docking and scoring combinations. Based on our benchmarking results, we established a hierarchical VS methodology and applied this approach to CLIP1-LTK, an oncogenic fusion protein lacking an experimentally resolved structure. Using this pipeline, a library of approximately three million compounds was virtually screened, leading to the identification of potential inhibitor candidates. Similarity-based analog searching identified QL07, which exhibited an IC 50 value of 524.27 nM. QL07 inhibited CLIP1-LTK downstream signaling pathways and induced apoptosis in transformed Ba/F3-CLIP1-LTK cells. Furthermore, QL07 suppressed the growth of CLIP1-LTK-positive tumors in xenograft models. These findings underscore the utility of AlphaFold models in overcoming structural limitations in drug discovery and demonstrate their feasibility in identifying promising small-molecule inhibitors against protein targets without experimentally-determined structures.

items.abstract: Protein kinases are key cellular regulators of growth, proliferation, and signal transduction, making them important therapeutic targets in precision medicine, particularly for cancer and inflammatory diseases. Although molecular docking remains a central tool in structure-based drug discovery, its predictive accuracy is often limited by rigid receptor assumptions and simplified solvent representation. To overcome these limitations, machine learning models were developed based on Extended Connectivity Interaction Features to predict kinase-ligand binding affinities. A kinase-specific dataset of 2337 complexes from PDBbind 2020 was used to train five regression models, namely Decision Tree, Support Vector Regressor, Gradient Boosting Regressor, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, using a merged descriptor set of 1757 interaction-specific and physicochemical features. Integration of RDKit descriptors consistently improved predictive performance across models. Among the evaluated models, GBR achieved the highest predictive correlation, with a PCC of 0.72 and R 2 value of 0.51, while SVR yielded the lowest mean squared error value of 0.84 with a PCC of 0.71. The XGBoost and RF followed with R 2 values of 0.49 and 0.42, respectively, whereas DT showed the weakest performance, with an R 2 value of 0.25 and a PCC of 0.54. External validation on 5265 complexes further confirmed the robustness of the framework and facilitated the identification of high-confidence binding candidates through consensus prediction. Notably, this strategy accurately predicted binding affinities and enabled prioritization of the top 20 compounds as potential kinase-binding leads, demonstrating a scalable and computationally efficient framework for improved virtual screening and hit prioritization in rational drug discovery.

items.abstract: Natural products derived from traditional medicines are valuable sources of potential geroprotective compounds; however, their translation into therapeutic candidates is limited by chemical complexity, polypharmacology, limited mechanistic resolution, and lengthy experimental validation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an emerging framework for integrating chemical, pharmacological, multi-omics, imaging, and literature derived data to accelerate natural product anti-aging research. This review summarizes recent applications of AI in three interconnected areas: drug repurposing, prediction of aging-related targets and signaling pathways, and identification of biomarkers for biological aging and cellular senescence. AI integrates chemical, molecular, omics, and imaging data to prioritize candidate compounds, predict drug-target interactions, identify synergistic combinations, and reveal mechanisms underlying geroprotection. However, computational predictions should not be interpreted as evidence of efficacy or causality. Data heterogeneity, sampling bias, limited model interpretability, inadequate external validation, and insufficient pharmacokinetic and long-term safety assessment remain major barriers to translation. Future progress will require an iterative framework that combines AI prediction with target engagement studies, senescence models, organoids, animal experiments, and clinical biomarker validation. This integrated strategy may improve the efficiency, reproducibility, and translational potential of natural product geroscience research.

items.abstract: AI models such as foundation models and generative models have shown promise for aiding drug discovery alongside traditional cheminformatics and bioinformatics tools and physics-based approaches. In this study, we design a workflow that integrates these AI methods to generate molecules alongside established informatic and predictive filtering approaches to streamline downselection of molecules from the massive and noisy result sets generated by AI. This workflow evaluates generative methods based on validity, reliability, diversity, similarity, hallucination and campaign needs. Analyses are made on the original proprietary dataset to determine molecular property thresholds for screening criteria. Overall, 249 molecules are selected from ~ 5 million generated molecules. 18 molecules are then validated with free energy perturbation simulations. 5 out of 5 retain on target inhibition, with IC 50 values below 1 μM. 1 of the 5 experimentally validated molecules displayed greater inhibition than the corresponding lead molecule. Predictive foundation model MMELON yields Pearson correlation R = 0.72 in blind test, showing potential for future drug discovery campaigns.

items.abstract: Chloroplast protein import components have been well documented in Arabidopsis and Chlamydomonas, but remain largely unexplored in other species. This is also true of the pea (Pisum sativum), a classic model system in which many of the early discoveries were made. This study provides an inventory of the components involved in the import of chloroplast proteins,and characterises the heterotrimeric translocon at the outer membrane of pea chloroplasts (TOC). We have identified a gateway in chloroplasts that is composed of TOC159, TOC75 and TOC34. Genome analysis revealed a single gene for each of TOC75 and TOC34, but multiple homologues of TOC159. This suggests that these genes are the primary determinants of the specificity of preproteins. Quantitative analysis of the chloroplast proteome demonstrates that TOC159-1 is dominant, implying a role in the photosynthesis-associated TOC complex (TOC-P). The TOC-P components are approximately three times more abundant than those of the 1MDa TIC complex. Quantitative mass spectrometry of isolated complexes also shows an excess of TOC-P over the 1MDa TICs, indicating separation of TOC and TIC. In a functional protein import assay, preRbcS co-isolated together with the TOC complex, demonstrating its preprotein receptor activity. AlphaFold 3 modelling suggests that dimers of the GTP-binding domains of TOC34 and TOC159-1 control access to a hybrid β-barrel assembly formed by the TOC75 and TOC159-1 β-barrel domains. These models also predict the presence of a transit peptide-binding groove within the TOC159 GTP-binding domain. Together, these findings contribute to a foundational model for TOC function in land plants.

items.abstract: Objective Ultrahigh-resolution (UHR) coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) using a photon-counting detector (PCD) provides excellent spatial resolution but is limited by increased image noise. We evaluated whether deep learning (DL)-based denoising and contrast enhancement can further improve UHR-CCTA image quality. Materials and methods UHR-CCTA scans from 25 patients with coronary artery disease were retrospectively analyzed. Images were reconstructed at 0.2-mm slice thickness without and with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR, Q off -Q 4 ), and subsequently processed using a DL tool for denoising and increasing iodine contrast enhancement. Subjective image quality (sharpness, noise, vessel wall delineation, and overall quality) was assessed by three radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale. Objective analysis included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and coronary wall sharpness. Differences between image sets were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results DL-based CCTA demonstrated significantly superior subjective image quality across all parameters compared to standard reconstructions, with an overall median image quality ([interquartile interval, IQR]: 4 [3-5] versus 2 [2-3], p < 0.001). SNR and CNR were significantly higher for DL-based CCTA across all QIR levels (all p < 0.001). The highest values were observed for DL-based CCTAQ 4 versus UHR-CCTAQ 4 (SNR: 258.0 ± 147.5 versus 145.2 ± 50.1; CNR: 25.8 ± 17.1 versus 11.1 ± 4.5; both p < 0.001). Coronary wall sharpness was improved for DL-based CCTA for Q 1-4 (all p < 0.027). Conclusion DL-based denoising and iodine contrast enhancement effectively reduce noise and improve anatomic detail in UHR-CCTA, providing incremental value beyond vendor-specific reconstruction, particularly at high QIR strength levels. Key points Question Deep learning reduces noise and enhances contrast in ultrahigh-resolution coronary CT angiography. Findings Image quality improves beyond standard iterative reconstruction methods, and vessel wall sharpness and diagnostic clarity significantly increase. Relevance statement This study aimed to determine at which levels of vendor-specific iterative reconstruction, DL-based denoising and contrast enhancement perform best in UHR CCTA, providing a foundation for future investigations on how these technical improvements may translate into diagnostic benefits.

items.abstract: Rationale and objectives Medical imaging typically generates 12-bit to 16-bit formats, yet conversion to 8-bit is often required. While deep learning has been widely explored in medical imaging, the influence of image bit depth on model performance is not fully understood. This study evaluates the impact of conversion from 16-bit to 8-bit for sex, age, and obesity classification using deep learning. Materials and methods In this retrospective, multi-institutional study, we analyzed 100,002 chest radiographs from 48,047 participants across three institutions. Images were uniformly quantized from the fixed 0-65535 range to 256 levels (0-255) with no additional processing. Three convolutional neural network architectures (ResNet52, EfficientNetB2, and ConvNeXtSmall) were trained on both 16-bit and 8-bit versions of the images. Model performance was evaluated using internal test datasets, randomly split multiple times, and an external test dataset. Statistical analysis included paired comparisons of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) values, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Results Across all architectures and classification tasks, differences between 16-bit and 8-bit model performance were minimal (mean differences ranging from -0.218%-0.184%). Statistical analyses revealed no significant differences in AUC-ROC values between bit depths for any model-task combination (all p values > 0.05 after Bonferroni correction). Effect sizes were small to moderate (Cohen's d ranging from -0.415-0.391). Conclusion No statistically significant differences were detected between models trained on 16-bit and 8-bit images in the three evaluated tasks. These findings suggest that conversion to 8-bit images may reduce data storage requirements and improve data processing efficiency. Further research is needed to assess their usefulness in clinical tasks.

items.abstract: Background and purpose Three-dimensional fast spin-echo MR cisternography (CUBE) of the internal auditory canal (IAC) and cerebellopontine angle (CPA) requires longer acquisition times that can limit clinical throughput. We evaluated whether a deep learning (DL)-based highly accelerated reconstruction technique, Sonic DL`™ (SDL), combined with a commercially available DL denoising reconstruction (AIR™ Recon DL, ARDL), preserves or improves subjective image quality and cochlear anatomy visualization relative to standard CUBE-ARDL while shortening scan time. Materials and methods Consecutive patients underwent brain MRI for suspected IAC pathology at 1.5T and 3T with paired acquisition of standard 3D CUBE-ARDL and an accelerated 3D CUBE-SDL sequence. Both used the same voxel size at 1.5T (0.6x0.6x1.2 mm 3 ) and 3T (0.6x0.6x0.6 mm 3 ). Scan times for CUBE-ARDL versus CUBE-SDL were 2:33 versus 1:41 min at 1.5T and 1:55 versus 1:11 min at 3T. Two independent neuroradiologists blinded to MRI acquisition method scored randomized, de-identified images on a 5-point Likert scale across five domains (overall image quality, noise, sharpness, artifacts, cochlear anatomy visualization). Reader-averaged scores for CUBE-ARDL and CUBE-SDL were compared with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with reader-specific and cumulative link mixed model (CLMM) sensitivity analyses and false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) quantified inter-reader reliability for each technique; Gwet's AC2 and weighted (Conger's) kappa with linear ordinal weights quantified pooled inter-reader agreement. Results After exclusion of 5 training cases per field strength, 49 (1.5T) and 34 (3T) patients were analyzed. CUBE-SDL scored significantly better than CUBE-ARDL for all five domains at both field strengths (all FDR-adjusted P < .001), consistently for each reader and in the CLMM. Inter-reader reliability (ICC) for CUBE-SDL was moderate-to-excellent at 3T (0.63-0.92) and moderate at 1.5T (0.65-0.74), generally exceeding CUBE-ARDL (3T: 0.35-0.61; 1.5T: 0.50-0.71). Pooled inter-reader agreement (Gwet's AC2) ranged from 0.56 to 0.89. Conclusions A combined Sonic DL acceleration with ARDL-denoised reconstruction for 3D T2 CUBE produced significantly higher subjective image quality at both 1.5T and 3T, and, at 3T, higher inter-reader reliability than standard CUBE-ARDL, while shortening acquisition time by 34%-38%. These findings support further evaluation, including diagnostic accuracy studies, of CUBE-SDL as an alternative to CUBE-ARDL.

items.abstract: Objectives Thyroid nodules are common and mostly benign, but 5-15% are malignant. Increasing detection rates may lead to overdiagnosis and unnecessary fine-needle aspiration biopsies (FNAB). We aimed to develop a machine learning (ML) model for thyroid malignancy risk assessment using ultrasound, FNAB, laboratory data and to compare its performance with the EU-TIRADS-PL reporting system. Methods This prospective study included 561 patients who underwent thyroidectomy based on preoperative ultrasound and FNAB results, including 261 malignant nodules (46.5%). Data were divided into training and test sets (3:1). Multiple ML algorithms were evaluated using clinical, sonographic, cytological and biochemical variables verified by histopathology. Results Logistic regression (LR) was selected as the final model because of its good performance and interpretability. The model achieved a test set ROC AUC of 74% and showed better correlation with thyroid malignancy than the EU-TIRADS-PL system. Significant predictors of malignancy included microcalcifications (p=0.002), younger age (p<0.001), male sex (p=0.001),and larger anteroposterior dimension (p=0.026). Larger longitudinal dimension was associated with lower malignancy risk (p<0.001). An anteroposterior-to-longitudinal dimension index was developed, with ROC AUC of 68% (95% CI 62.0-71.0). Conclusions The proposed ML model showed good accuracy and may improve thyroid malignancy risk assessment compared with systems based only on sonographic features.

items.abstract: Background The choroid plexus is essential for brain homeostasis, yet its in vivo morphology remains incompletely characterized. Conventional MRI visualizes only part of the choroid plexus and may therefore misrepresent age- and disease-related structural changes. We aim to develop a 7T contrast-enhanced black-blood imaging (CeBBI) framework for whole-brain visualization and quantitative morphologic characterization of the choroid plexus, and to examine its associations with aging and cerebrovascular disease. Methods We retrospectively included 234 participants referred for evaluation of intracranial atherosclerotic disease who underwent CeBBI. A deep learning model was trained to segment the whole choroid plexus. Choroid plexus volume, centerline-based shape features and cystic components were quantified. Segmentations derived from CeBBI were compared with those obtained using a validated T1-weighted MRI-based method. Associations with age, ventricular size and vascular imaging markers were assessed. Results 7T CeBBI enabled visualization of the choroid plexus across all ventricular compartments. The segmentation model achieved high accuracy (Dice score=0.901±0.013), and recovered more than twice the choroid plexus volume detected by the T1-weighted method. Total choroid plexus volume was not associated with age. However, with advancing age, the lateral ventricular choroid plexus became shorter (left r=-0.250, right r=-0.303, both P<0.001) and showed greater cross-sectional area (left r=0.174, right r=0.176, both P=0.007). Choroid plexus cyst number (r=0.187, P=0.004) and cyst volume (r=0.159, P=0.015) also increased with age. Cerebral microbleeds were independently associated with greater lateral ventricular choroid plexus volume (standardized β=0.178, P=0.012). Conclusions Our method enables robust whole-brain visualization and quantitative morphologic assessment of the choroid plexus. Rather than undergoing simple age-related hypertrophy, the choroid plexus showed complex remodeling characterized by shortening, cross-sectional expansion and cystic change. The association between cerebral microbleeds and larger choroid plexus volume further supports a potential role of vascular dysfunction in choroid plexus remodeling.

items.abstract: Background This study aimed to validate the effectiveness of a deep learning-based point cloud completion method for the reverse reconstruction of the patient-specific anatomy of the knee bone morphology, thereby providing technical support for personalized diagnosis and treatment. Methods A computed tomography (CT) database containing 140 normal knees was constructed. There were 10 clinically common defect patterns (7 femoral, 3 tibial) generated. Multiple deep learning methods were employed to achieve defect point cloud completion. Virtual testing was conducted to compare the morphological consistency (assessed by Chamfer Distance, Density-Aware Chamfer Distance, and F-score) and anatomical parameter consistency between the resulting and original intact models. The optimal point cloud completion method, based on the evaluation results, was selected for preliminary clinical feasibility testing. Consistency between reconstructed affected-side models and the intact contralateral knee models was assessed in patients who have unilateral post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Results In virtual testing, the CRA-PCN deep learning model yielded the best reconstruction performance. For all defect patterns, the reconstructed geometries attained a chamfer distance below 0.45 mm, while deviations of anatomical parameters were limited to within 0.5 mm for linear measurements and 0.2° for angular measurements. In the preliminary clinical feasibility testing, the reconstructed morphology exhibited a chamfer distance of approximately 1.2 mm compared to the contralateral side. The restoration accuracy of the joint line angle was superior in extensive defect patterns, with the optimal deviation being within 0.2° on the femoral side and approximately 0.7° on the tibial side. Conclusion The CRA-PCN model enables reverse reconstruction of defective knee structures with satisfactory anatomical restoration. It provides quantitative anatomical references for personalized arthroplasty and aids identification of deformity origins in osteoarthritis (OA) patients, though further large-scale prospective research is required to verify its clinical value.

items.abstract: Personalised radioligand therapy (RLT) depends on accurate absorbed-dose estimation. Standard dosimetry requires multiple post-therapy single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) acquisitions, imposing logistical burdens. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have been proposed to streamline organ segmentation, generate synthetic imaging timepoints, and predict patient-specific doses. We evaluated the performance, methodological quality, and translational readiness of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven dosimetry in the clinical theranostics literature. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and regional databases (Jan 1, 2014, to March 1, 2025). Studies applying AI to dosimetry in human RLT recipients were eligible. Two reviewers screened and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed with the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST) and the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2). Meta-analyses of organ segmentation (Dice similarity coefficient [DSC]) and dose prediction (concordance correlation coefficient [CCC]) used restricted maximum-likelihood (REML) random-effects models restricted to studies with independent validation sets. CRD420261349805 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=1349805). 58 studies met inclusion criteria covering 1847 patients (1523 [82%] male, 324 [18%] female). 23 studies with independent validation were eligible for meta-analysis. Pooled DSC was 0·87 (95% CI 0·83-0·90; 16 studies). Pooled voxel dosimetry relative absolute error (RAE) was 6·1% (4·6-8·1%; 12 studies). Pretherapy kidney dose prediction yielded pooled CCC 0·79 (0·72-0·85; 8 studies). PROBAST identified high risk of bias in 71% of prediction studies. Reducing timepoints from ≥3 to 1-2 scans increased RAE by 8·2 percentage points (5·1-11·4). AI reduced median processing time from 180 to 25 minutes. On independent validation data, AI-driven dosimetry shows promising accuracy for organ-level dose estimation and substantially reduces processing time. However, the evidence base remains immature: 71% of prediction studies carry high risk of bias, only four studies report external validation, and most pooled outcomes were graded as low or very low certainty. External multicentre validation and prospective randomised trials comparing AI-guided against fixed-activity RLT are needed before clinical adoption. Current evidence primarily demonstrates technical feasibility rather than proven clinical utility.

items.abstract: Preoperative knowledge of intracranial meningioma grade could significantly enhance surgical planning, but reliable noninvasive prediction remains an unmet clinical need. The aim of this study was to develop and externally validate a machine learning (ML) model incorporating traditional radiomic features, along with novel fractal and topological features, to predict WHO meningioma grade from preoperative MRI using a large multicenter cohort. This retrospective diagnostic study analyzed a cohort of patients in the BraTS Meningioma Challenge. Patient data (n = 909) from 6 academic medical centers were used for model training and internal validation (n = 699) and one-time final external validation (n = 210). Tumors were segmented into three regions and radiomic features extracted across four MRI sequences. Eight different ML algorithms (e.g., based on neural networks, decision trees, clustering, and linear relationships) were tested across a total of 2889 candidate features. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for prediction of binarized WHO grade (1 vs 2 or 3). The final model used a support vector machine algorithm comprising 20 features and achieved an AUROC of 0.824 (95% CI 0.755-0.883) on unseen test data, with favorable calibration. Feature importance analysis revealed that topological complexity added complementary predictive value to conventional radiomics features. The final model is publicly available for anyone to use. This externally validated ML model accurately predicted meningioma grade using routine preoperative MRI, with the potential to guide surgical decision-making and serve as a basis for future imaging-based brain tumor classifications.

items.abstract: Head and neck (HN) cancer survivorship is associated with persistent symptom burden and long-term brain-behavioral health alterations, yet mechanisms underlying brain aging remain poorly understood. We investigated whether HN cancer survivors exhibit accelerated brain aging, whether limbic white matter (WM) pathways contribute to these changes, and whether measures associated with glymphatic function are associated with reduced brain aging. Diffusion MRI and symptom burden data were analyzed in 135 HN cancer survivors and compared with a normative cohort from the Human Connectome Project (n = 1,228). Two machine learning models (elastic net [ENET] and random forest [RF]) using fractional anisotropy (FA) and quantitative anisotropy (QA) from 45 WM tracts were trained to estimate brain age and compute brain age gap (BAG). Glymphatic-related processes were indirectly assessed using diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular spaces (DTI-ALPS). Moderation analyses examined whether symptom burden influenced associations among DTI-ALPS, BAG, and WM integrity. Survivors showed a negative mean BAG of -1.64 years in the ENET model, indicating a nonsignificant tendency toward delayed brain aging, whereas the RF model showed a positive mean BAG of 3.59 years, indicating accelerated brain aging. The RF model demonstrated stronger external generalizability and greater biological coherence, including associations with ALPS and symptom-related measures. The bilateral fornix and right U-fibers were among the strongest contributors to RF-based brain age prediction. Higher DTI-ALPS index values were associated with lower BAG and greater fornix integrity, particularly in survivors with lower symptom burden and reduced activity-related interference. HN cancer survivorship was associated with accelerated brain aging in the model demonstrating greater external generalizability and biological relevance, alongside alterations in limbic WM pathways. Higher DTI-ALPS was associated with reduced brain aging, with symptom burden modifying this relationship. These findings highlight brain health as an important component of cancer survivorship.

items.abstract: Cystic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (c-PanNETs) are an uncommon cystic phenotype of well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, accounting for approximately 7-12% of PanNETs in several surgical series, although reported frequencies vary according to the definition of cystic morphology and cohort selection. Retrospective studies suggest that c-PanNETs may exhibit less aggressive clinicopathologic features than their solid counterparts; however, their imaging appearance frequently overlaps with other pancreatic cystic neoplasms, particularly branch-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, mucinous cystic neoplasms, and atypical serous cystic neoplasms. Accurate preoperative recognition may have important implications for patient management and surgical planning. This review summarizes the imaging features of c-PanNETs across computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, as well as the complementary roles of endoscopic ultrasound and somatostatin receptor PET/CT. Particular attention is given to arterial hyperenhancement of the cyst wall, septations, mural nodules, or residual solid components; assessment of communication with the main pancreatic duct; and integration of complementary imaging findings. Because these features are not specific, their interpretation in combination with lesion morphology and ductal relationships is emphasized. Practical approaches to differential diagnosis and common interpretive pitfalls are also discussed. The review further addresses emerging quantitative imaging techniques, including radiomics and artificial intelligence, while recognizing that evidence specific to c-PanNETs remains limited. A practical diagnostic algorithm and structured reporting checklist are provided to support systematic interpretation and multidisciplinary communication. Recognition of the imaging spectrum of c-PanNETs, combined with systematic assessment of enhancement characteristics, ductal anatomy, and complementary imaging findings, may improve diagnostic confidence and support appropriate patient management.

items.abstract: Achieving tight glycemic control in Type 1 diabetes is challenged by non-linear metabolic dynamics and insulin-stacking risk. Artificial intelligence models offer improved personalization, but their opacity raises safety concerns, particularly for basal insulin dosing, which is often treated as static in existing decision-support systems. We propose a hybrid closed-loop system combining a data-driven LightGBM regressor for basal dose prediction, trained on the T1D-UOM dataset, with a physiologically grounded, rule-based safety layer at the edge. Basal insulin is predicted from cyclical time encoding and glucose rate-of-change; bolus dosing follows carbohydrate intake and correction requirements. A time-bounded insulin-on-board model, an uncertainty-adaptive post-bolus damping factor, and a predictive low-glucose-suspend rule reproducing the Tandem Basal-IQ protocol together suspend or reduce delivery when residual insulin is high or hypoglycemia is projected. The system was evaluated in silico over 60 continuous days under shadow-mode replay and closed-loop reduced-order simulation, including an ablation with bolus delivery suppressed. Under chronological, within-subject validation, the offline basal estimator achieved R2=0.68 and MAE=0.21 U; under strict leave-one-subject-out validation on the same real cohort, performance did not generalize to unseen subjects ( R2=-0.49 , MAE=0.49 U). The hybrid controller maintained Time-in-Range at 62.8% within the reduced-order closed-loop simulation, with no violations of the insulin-on-board suspension or damping rules; suppressing bolus delivery in an ablation within this simulation dropped Time-in-Range to 26.1%, indicating that, within the reduced-order model, bolus delivery is a determinant of simulated glycemic outcome. The proposed architecture demonstrates a safety-audited template for combining machine-learning basal prediction with clinically grounded dosing rules. Validation on real outcome data and physical hardware is identified as the next steps toward clinical translation.

items.abstract: Acromegaly has an insidious onset and prolonged diagnostic delay. Vocal changes are a recognized clinical feature, the diagnostic value of deep learning architectures remains underexplored. We aimed to assess Wav2Vec2.0-based voice analysis as a non-invasive digital biomarker for acromegaly. This single-center case-control study included 70 patients with acromegaly and 68 age- and sex-matched controls. Clinical status was defined by standard biochemical criteria, symptoms, comorbidities, and residual tumor. Voice samples were recorded with a standard mobile phone and resampled to 16 kHz. Wav2Vec2.0 was used to extract high-dimensional embedding vectors. These embeddings, were used to train and validate four different machine learning classifiers using an 80%/20% train-test split with five-fold cross-validation. Model calibration was assessed with the Brier score, and clinical utility with decision curve analysis (DCA). Demographics were similar between acromegaly (mean age 45.5 years; 57.1% female) and control (mean age 47.5 years; 61.8% female) groups. On the internal hold-out test set, Logisitic Regression model maintained high accuracy (AUC 0.84; specificity 0.92; sensitivity 0.71) and showed good calibration [Brier score 0.165 (95% CI 0.057-0.289)]. DCA confirmed that LR provided the highest benefit across a clinically relevant range of threshold probabilities (~ 15-85%). items.abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate OPXrayNet, an automated deep-learning framework for opportunistic osteoporosis (OP) screening using multi-site skeletal X-ray images, to address the limitations of single-site analysis and poor interpretability in existing methods. This retrospective, multicenter diagnostic study utilized 16,347 annotated X-ray images from 2186 patients. The reference standard was OP diagnosis based on DXA T-score (≤ -2.5). OPXrayNet integrated YOLOv8 for automated region-of-interest detection, a spatial-frequency joint focusing architecture for feature enhancement, a feature pyramid network for multi-scale fusion, and an expert-guided loss module. Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated using accuracy and AUC, comparing performance against models including DeepSeek-VL2 and DCNN via statistical tests on internal and external validation sets. The study included 2186 participants (mean age 69.0 ± 10.5 years; 72.3% female). On the internal test set (n = 3892), OPXrayNet achieved an accuracy of 80.1%; observed accuracy values for baseline models were lower. On the external validation set, it attained an AUC of 0.844 (95% CI: 0.821-0.867); a numerical difference of 3.9% was observed when compared with other models. Feature heatmaps suggest that the model focuses on clinically critical bone structures. OPXrayNet effectively provides accurate, automated, and interpretable opportunistic OP screening from multi-site X-ray images, showing promising performance for scalable clinical application in primary care settings. Question There is a notable absence of automated, interpretable, and highly accurate deep learning methodologies for conducting opportunistic OP screening using multi-site X-ray images. Findings The OPXrayNet model achieved an accuracy of 80.1% and an AUC of 0.844 in automated OP screening across multi-site X-rays in internal and external validation cohorts; numerical differences in performance metrics were observed when compared with baseline models. Clinical relevance This framework offers an accurate, automated, and interpretable screening tool for OP using routine X-rays, presenting substantial potential for scalable clinical application in primary care. It enables early detection without incurring additional costs or radiation exposure.

items.abstract: Spatial proteomics enables high-resolution mapping of protein expression within the tumor microenvironment, but its routine clinical application remains limited by cost, technical complexity and restricted tissue coverage. Here we present Hist2Prot, a deep learning framework that generates single-cell spatial proteomic profiles from routine hematoxylin and eosin histology. Trained on approximately 51 million paired cells from a same-section G4X spatial proteomics dataset, Hist2Prot was evaluated in internal test cohorts, independent same-platform G4X cohorts and external cross-platform datasets comprising approximately 72 million additional cells, showing concordance with measured protein profiles and outperforming established baselines. Hist2Prot-derived virtual proteins preserved immune, stromal and tumor cell phenotypes and recapitulated clinically relevant tumor microenvironment organization. Across seven independent patient cohorts comprising 1,774 patients, virtual spatial proteomics improved molecular biomarker, prognostic and immunotherapy response prediction beyond hematoxylin and eosin morphology alone. Hist2Prot enables scalable single-cell computational spatial proteomics from routine histology for precision oncology.

items.abstract: A new generation of medicines that includes gene therapies, cell-based treatments and gene editors have the potential to treat a vast range of diseases. However, the clinical success of these novel modalities is limited by unwanted immune responses, which can compromise both safety and efficacy. Regulatory agencies have recently emphasized reducing animal testing in preclinical safety studies and envisioned a strategic approach for basing regulatory decisions on scientifically validated new approach methodologies (NAMs). These methods encompass mathematical models, artificial intelligence tools, organ-on-a-chip systems, and advanced in vitro and ex vivo assays. In combination, these approaches seem potentially well suited for assessing unwanted immune responses of the novel modalities. Key challenges to be addressed include predicting the immunogenicity risks from transgene products, delivery vehicles and gene-editing machinery; managing pre-existing immunity; overcoming barriers to repeat dosing; and establishing robust long-term monitoring strategies. In this Perspective, we critically evaluate how the current NAMs toolkit, originally developed for protein therapeutics, can be adapted to assess the unwanted immune responses of novel modalities. We provide a forward-looking framework for developing and validating the next generation of predictive immunogenicity tools required to safely unlock the full therapeutic potential of these revolutionary medicines.

items.abstract: Precision oncology based on the identification of actionable genomic alterations (AGAs) has been transformative in the care of solid tumors, yet optimal treatment selection is often hindered by tissue exhaustion and slow turnaround times. Artificial intelligence (AI) addresses these barriers by predicting AGAs directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides. Recent landmark studies, including the prospective EAGLE and ANNAR trials, have demonstrated that deep learning models can identify alterations such as EGFR in non-small cell lung cancer and FGFR in urothelial cancer across diverse global cohorts. By providing near-instant, non-destructive results, AI-based prediction can triage patients for molecular testing or clinical trials at the time of initial diagnosis. This perspective evaluates the maturing evidence base and outlines a pragmatic pathway for integrating these tools into clinical practice. Ultimately, these models offer the opportunity to extract critical molecular information from slides generated in every laboratory worldwide and to significantly improve timely access to the rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape of solid tumors.

items.abstract: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are essential to understanding how people live with illness, treatment, and care, and are increasingly promoted for routine use in clinical practice, quality improvement, and value-based health care. PROs are also increasingly relevant in digital health and artificial intelligence applications, both as inputs to predictive models and as outputs reflecting patient-centred aspects of health. Yet, PROs remain difficult to reuse at scale: their implementation is inconsistent across health-care settings, measurement approaches are highly heterogeneous, and PROs are rarely available as large, standardised, analysable datasets suitable for multisite analyses and advanced analytics, including artificial intelligence models. In this Viewpoint, we argue that the central challenge is not a lack of initiatives, but the absence of a coherent, end-to-end approach that connects measurement, routine capture, data standards, and analytic reuse. We propose a practical four-step pathway towards Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) PROs. This pathway focuses on (1) defining the outcome domains that matter and selecting high-quality questionnaires; (2) capturing PROs consistently at the point of care in structured, computable formats; (3) storing them in analysable, shareable data models; and (4) establishing transparent cross-questionnaire linking to enable comparable scores. None of these steps poses major technical challenges in isolation; the primary difficulty is that these efforts are often developed in silos, with minimal coordination across disciplines, from questionnaire development and validation to clinical workflows, informatics standards, analytic infrastructures, and governance. A shared FAIR-PROs approach would allow PROs to become a routine, reusable component of learning health systems and a driver of both person-centred care and data-driven innovation.

items.abstract: Selected laryngeal voice disorders represent a significant clinical challenge, motivating the development of non-invasive, accurate, and interpretable screening support systems. In this study, the proposed framework is developed and evaluated using three dataset-defined voice categories: Laryngocele, Vox senilis (presbyphonia), and Normal. Although recent machine learning approaches have demonstrated strong classification performance, many remain limited by their black-box nature and limited decision-support capabilities. This study proposes a preliminary explainable and decision-oriented Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework for voice screening using selected acoustic features. The methodology integrates acoustic feature extraction from voice recordings with Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and a Random Forest classifier. To enhance interpretability, the framework incorporates both local and global explainability through Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), enabling examination of the contribution of acoustic features such as Glottal-to-Noise Excitation (GNE) and fundamental-frequency (F₀) characteristics to model predictions. In addition, counterfactual reasoning is introduced through the Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) method to illustrate how hypothetical feature-level modifications can influence predictive outcomes. A key component is the proposed Agentic Voice Disorder Diagnosis Agent (AVDD-Agent), which integrates predictive outputs, explainability, and author-defined rule-based reasoning to provide feature analysis, confidence-based risk assessment, and general voice-health and follow-up guidance. Experimental evaluation demonstrates classification performance across the three investigated dataset-defined categories, supported by statistical analyses using t tests, ANOVA (F = 60.2404, P < 0.001), and chi-square tests. The proposed framework integrates prediction, interpretability, counterfactual analysis, and decision support, demonstrating the feasibility of preliminary explainable Agentic AI-based voice screening within the scope of the investigated dataset.

items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into healthcare offers significant potential for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and personalised medicine, yet carries inherent risks including algorithmic bias, opacity, and threats to patient safety and fundamental rights. These concerns demand robust governance frameworks that transcend aspirational recommendations. This article examines the role of ex ante evaluation in ensuring compliance with ethical and regulatory standards for AI systems in healthcare, using the PIO Model (Principles, Indicators, and Observables) as an illustrative case study. The PIO Model on Health provides a structured self-assessment methodology grounded in the European Commission's ethical principles for trustworthy AI while aligning with binding legal obligations under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the Medical Devices Regulation, and the General Data Protection Regulation. Built around the operational question "Have we done it?", the Model enables stakeholders to critically evaluate AI systems through a comprehensive checklist organised according to seven ethical principles: transparency; justice and fairness; security and non-maleficence; responsibility; privacy; autonomy; and sustainability. The paper frames AI in healthcare within the human rights framework, examining risks including algorithmic bias, automation bias, erosion of the patient-physician relationship, and challenges posed by generative AI such as hallucinations and data protection concerns. The PIO Model performs an essential ex ante evaluation function, enabling identification of ethical and legislative deficiencies prior to formal conformity assessment or market placement. It facilitates continuous monitoring through medical algorithmic audit, generating metrics including conformity percentages, risk matrices, and improvement catalogues that serve as actionable guides for implementing corrective measures. Designed for collective administration incorporating technical, clinical, legal, and ethics experts alongside patient representatives, the Model synthesises proliferating ethical guidelines and complex regulatory requirements into an operational instrument that transcends minimum legal standards, contributing to developing trustworthy AI systems that safeguard patient welfare and fundamental rights.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing nanomedicine development by linking formulation variables and biological context with delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and safety. This review examines AI assisted formulation design, centralized formulation databases, prediction of nanoparticle self assembly, and models of cell and tissue selective delivery, biodistribution, and therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in predicting nanotoxicity and nanoparticle induced immune responses further emphasize the importance of incorporating safety endpoints into nanomedicine optimization. Beyond nanocarrier engineering, foundation models and multimodal analyses of single-cell and spatial data are expanding biological discovery by characterizing disease associated cellular states, prioritizing therapeutic targets, and predicting treatment responses. Computational approaches also support the design of therapeutic RNA, peptides, proteins, and programmable protein nanomaterials. For example, mRNA sequences generated by GEMORNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles increased erythropoietin expression in mice by up to 15-fold compared with a benchmark sequence. Integration of biological discovery with biomolecular and nanocarrier design may inform therapeutic cargo selection, targeting strategies, and functional nanomaterial development. AI may connect patient specific biological characteristics with predictions of nanomedicine delivery and therapeutic response to support patient stratification and individualized treatment selection. Integration of histological, imaging, molecular, and longitudinal data may enable treatment strategies to be adapted to differences in tissue characteristics, disease state, and therapeutic response. Emerging approaches based on digital twins and adaptive treatment control may extend the framework toward individualized dosing and dynamic treatment optimization. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, limited model generalizability, and the need for experimental and prospective validation. Progress toward precision therapy will require integrated frameworks that jointly consider delivery, efficacy, selectivity, and safety while clearly distinguishing demonstrated applications from future opportunities.

items.abstract: Objective rare interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by various pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentations, prognoses, and therapeutic challenges. Among these, acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) exemplify rare pulmonary diseases driven by distinct biological mechanisms, including lysosomal dysfunction, impaired surfactant homeostasis, and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) pathways. Recent advancements in molecular biology, genomics, and translational research boosted the development of precision medicine strategies and disease-specific therapies for these conditions. Study design this narrative review was conducted in accordance with the SANRA guidelines. A thorough literature search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases was performed from January 2000 to June 2026. Results significant progress has been made in treating all three diseases. In ASMD, enzyme replacement therapy with olipudase alfa has greatly improved visceral and lung symptoms, while research in gene therapy, gene editing, and metabolic treatments is ongoing. For PAP, inhaled granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is now the primary disease-specific treatment, now supported by phase III trial evidence for inhaled molgramostim, complemented by potential therapies such as immunomodulation, macrophage transplantation, and gene-based strategies. In PLCH, the discovery of recurrent MAPK pathway variants has supported the use of genotype-targeted treatments with BRAF and MEK inhibitors. Under these conditions, advances in molecular diagnostics, circulating biomarkers, quantitative HRCT, radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to enhance diagnosis, patient stratification, prognosis, and treatment decisions. Conclusions ASMD, PAP and PLCH are entering into an era of precision medicine, in which disease-specific molecular mechanisms play an increasing role in guiding diagnosis and treatment. Ongoing integration of genomics, biomarkers, advanced imaging, AI, and targeted therapies could revolutionise the management of conditions such as ASMD, PAP, and PLCH, leading to better long-term patient outcomes.
