items.abstract: Many of the most consequential advances promised by AI, from curing diseases and inventing new technologies to formulating new scientific theories, are fundamentally creative acts. Yet creativity is uniquely difficult to learn because it faces a creative paradox: learning to repeat past examples of creative success makes those specific examples more likely to recur, inhibiting the very creativity desired. This work argues that creativity is better modeled as an explicit process rather than as a property of individual artifacts, and proposes to learn the underlying generative principles behind the creative process. In particular, to escape the paradox, we introduce creative priming (CP), wherein a trained priming model generates a prompt-specific primer that assists a response model in being creative, explicitly decoupling the creative process from response generation. The priming model learns through GRPO, rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse, thereby reinforcing the process that yields creative responses without reinforcing any specific response.

items.title: Click3R: Interactive Stereo 3D Reconstruction with Sparse Correspondence Clicks
items.summary: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point…
items.abstract: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.

items.title: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment
items.summary: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment…
items.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.

items.title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization
items.summary: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish…
items.abstract: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

items.title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
items.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. items.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.

items.title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
items.summary: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from…
items.abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π_{0.5} and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.

items.title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time
items.summary: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's…
items.abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.

items.title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery
items.summary: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI…
items.abstract: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.

items.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

items.title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its…
items.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

items.title: LO-World: Unified BEV Latent Modeling for Joint 4D Occupancy and LiDAR Forecasting
items.summary: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we…
items.abstract: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose LO-World, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding 25~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzzzzzm/LO-World.

items.title: Embodied First Exam
items.summary: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where…
items.abstract: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.

items.title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
items.summary: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates…
items.abstract: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

items.summary: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. items.abstract: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

items.title: GPCRAgent: an intelligent multi-agent platform integrating knowledge graphs and large language models for GPCR-targeted drug discovery.
items.summary: Introduction G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major therapeutic targets in drug discovery. However, systematic characterization of GPCR functions and ligand interactions remains constrained by the high cost and complexity of experimental approaches. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in biomedical question answering, their direct application to GPCR research is limited by…
items.abstract: Introduction G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major therapeutic targets in drug discovery. However, systematic characterization of GPCR functions and ligand interactions remains constrained by the high cost and complexity of experimental approaches. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in biomedical question answering, their direct application to GPCR research is limited by insufficient integration of structured domain knowledge and poor interpretability of generated inferences. Objectives This study aimed to develop an interpretable artificial intelligence framework for automated and traceable analysis of complex GPCR-related problems, and to evaluate its utility in GPCR knowledge reasoning, structural property interpretation, disease target prioritization and ligand recommendation. Methods We developed GPCRAgent, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework enabled by VecKG-CoReason, which integrates vector-based semantic retrieval with knowledge graph-guided collaborative reasoning. GPCRAgent was evaluated on benchmark tasks covering GPCR knowledge question answering, multiple-choice reasoning and structural property interpretation. Its practical utility was further assessed in an idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis case study, in which prioritized targets and ligand candidates were supported by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. Results GPCRAgent achieved accuracies of 85 % in GPCR knowledge question answering, 90 % in multiple-choice reasoning and 83 % in structural property interpretation, outperforming general-purpose LLMs across benchmark tasks. In an idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis case study, GPCRAgent identified LPAR1 as the top candidate and prioritized potential ligands. In a separate renal fibrosis study, experimental evaluation of the optimized LPAR1 ligand in kidney organoids showed suppressed fibrosis-associated marker induction for IL-1β-induced fibrosis. These results illustrate how the platform integrates evidence for target prioritization and structure-based ligand assessment. To facilitate broader application, an online platform (https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/GPCRAgent/) was developed to support GPCR-related drug discovery. Conclusion By integrating structured knowledge retrieval with collaborative multi-agent reasoning, GPCRAgent provides an interpretable AI framework for evidence-based GPCR target prioritization, ligand recommendation, and decision support.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce NarrativeBench, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. NarrativeBench provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

items.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \hivemem, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textsc{H}or\textsc{i}zontal Memory Expansion with \textsc{Ve}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.

items.abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody–antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

items.abstract: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.

items.abstract: While Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) accelerates isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, distributed LLM training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels, and communication schedules, where single edits often hit out-of-memory (OOM) boundaries, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter, or silent numerical drift. We present InfraRSI, the agentic harness that turns open-ended human commands into verified training optimizations via a five-stage workflow: init locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss, and timing invariants to prevent reward hacking, doctor profiles baseline phases and calibrates cluster noise, run co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches before re-verifying top candidates against the baseline and logging findings to a cross-hardware experience bank, and report and apply audit source paths, track failed-trial costs, and commit promoted changes. Rather than stepping greedily from a single incumbent, InfraRSI initializes from diverse experience-seeded configurations and fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials, including OOMs. Using these models, it prices per-setting memory costs, revises miscalibrated LLM priors from live runs, and pairs memory-hungry optimizations with memory savers and verified code patches. Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to 2.75times and lifts mean Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from 17.4% to 30.0%, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs. As it improves training infrastructure efficiency, InfraRSI forms a two-level Recursive Self-Improvement loop---revising priors online within runs and distilling experience across clusters---to push foundation model scaling.

items.abstract: Manual localization of anatomical landmarks within human cochlea structures in 3D computed tomography (CT) images is labor-intensive. However, despite progress in various studies on automatic localization methods, it remains challenging to jointly achieve rapid, precise, and fully automated landmark localization. Therefore, we propose a deep learning-based localization framework, called MEDICO-YOLO, which bridges speed and precision. It can automatically and simultaneously localize 6 human cochlea landmarks (apex, basal point, round window center of both left and right cochleae) in the full-resolution 3D CT images. The main contributions are: 1) MEDICO-YOLO learns from few manually annotated 3D CT images; 2) Within the framework, a 2D CNN-based network was developed to specifically localize cochlea landmarks in 3D single-scale medical CT images; 3) A novel loss function was designed; 4) The localization model achieved human expert-level precision while ensuring rapid inference. This study employed anonymized 3D pre-operative CT images (0.3 mm, covering the full head or temporal bone region). The evaluation involved comparing four models that were trained using 4 different training set sizes (n=4, 8, 12, 16). Each of them was evaluated on a distinct test set (n=16). The results show that the MEDICO-YOLO framework achieved strong localization performance by learning from few annotated 3D CT images. Trained on only 8 CT volumes, the model already attained a mean localization error of 1.30 mm (approximately 4 voxels). When trained on 16 CT volumes, the model achieved a mean error of 0.71 mm and a successful detection rate (SDR@3.0 mm) of 97.92%. Furthermore, on an Apple M1 laptop, the model achieved a real-time speed (32 ms) for inferencing each 2D slice (608 x 608) and an average latency of 25.43 s for inferencing the full 3D CT image (608 x 608 x 200, including post-processing). The complete methodology for the MEDICO-YOLO framework is presented in this article.

items.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) scans are a widely available yet underused resource that can be leveraged for opportunistic osteoporosis screening. This study aimed to develop sex- and site-specific reference curves for volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) to define dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-anchored percentile thresholds for osteoporosis classification, and to evaluate whether these thresholds identified individuals who subsequently sustain a major osteoporotic fracture (MOF). A retrospective cohort of 4,418 clinical CT scans was analyzed, including a subset of 1,088 scans with corresponding DXA imaging within one year. MOF incidence and timing following CT were obtained from linked administrative health data. CT images were segmented with deep learning models to extract the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and femoral neck from which vBMDs were assessed using internal calibration. Sex-specific vBMD centile curves were generated for each region using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape. A receiver operating characteristic analysis with the Youden index defined percentile thresholds that aligned with DXA-defined osteoporosis. Clinical relevance was assessed by determining the proportion of participants classified as osteoporotic by the CT-derived percentile thresholds who subsequently sustained a MOF, and by evaluating the association between CT-defined osteoporosis and time to incident fracture using Cox proportional hazards models. The cohort included 2,368 males and 2,050 females. At the vertebral body, 66.3% (n=67) of female and 41.9% (n=26) of male fracture cases had vBMD values below the CT-defined osteoporosis threshold, consistent with osteoporosis. Among these, 44.8% (n=30) of females and 76.9% (n=20) of males had not undergone DXA screening. Individuals classified as osteoporotic based on CT-derived thresholds had up to 2.86 times higher risk of sustaining an MOF across all vertebral sites in both sexes. These findings indicate that CT-derived vBMD percentile thresholds offer clinically meaningful cut-points for opportunistic screening and support their use as a diagnostic flag for further evaluation.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be used by patients and caregivers to answer medical questions and the characterization of safety concerns in LLM outputs for patient-facing applications is an active area of research. In this work, we study LLM responses to caregiver questions about hyperglycemia in pediatric type 1 diabetes. We measure the frequency of a potential safety failure: advice to dose insulin in the absence of a clear warning to account for insulin-on-board. We found occurrences of the potential safety failure across four LLMs tested through programmatic endpoints and two LLMs tested through chat interfaces. The rates of the potential safety failure varied when different context was given about the patient's meal and insulin history and treatment regimen. These results highlight a need for guardrails for patients with diabetes who use LLMs to manage their care.

items.title: Methodological Adherence, Reporting Completeness, and Risk of Bias in AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews: A Matched Meta-Research Study
items.summary: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate systematic reviews that inform clinical practice and policy. However, evidence on the methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias of completed AI–assisted reviews is limited. Objective: To compare methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias between published systematic reviews with reported AI…
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate systematic reviews that inform clinical practice and policy. However, evidence on the methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias of completed AI–assisted reviews is limited. Objective: To compare methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias between published systematic reviews with reported AI assistance and matched reviews with no reported AI use, and to assess AI–use transparency. Methods: We conducted a matched–cohort meta–research study of English–language, peer–reviewed health systematic reviews. AI–assisted reviews published during 2023—2025 were matched 1:2 to reviews with no reported AI use using individualized MEDLINE searches targeting publication timing, clinical domain, review type, and meta-analysis status. When more than two eligible comparators were available, two were randomly selected. AI assistance was defined as reported use during searching, screening, data extraction, risk–of–bias assessment, evidence synthesis, or substantive drafting. Full texts and supplementary materials were examined to classify reported AI use. The primary outcome was a prespecified modified 13–item AMSTAR–2 methodological–adherence score (range 0 — 13; noninferiority margin &−1 point). Secondary outcomes included PRISMA 2020 reporting completeness and ROBIS risk of bias; AI–use transparency was assessed descriptively. Adapted 13–item AMSTAR–2 confidence categories were summarized descriptively, while critical– and noncritical–domain adherence was examined in exploratory adjusted analyses. Multivariable regression models adjusted for journal impact tier, funding reporting, formal review–group affiliation, review–team size, and review–question type, using cluster–robust standard errors by matched set. Sensitivity analyses included matched–set fixed–effects models. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q5JRW). Results: The cohort included 231 systematic reviews: 77 AI–assisted and 154 with no reported AI use. Mean 13–item AMSTAR–2 scores were 7.58 and 9.63, respectively. In multivariable–adjusted analyses, AI–assisted reviews scored 1.64 points lower (95% CI &−2.37 to &− 0.91); noninferiority was not demonstrated. PRISMA adherence was estimated to be 4.7 percentage points lower among AI-assisted reviews in primary adjusted analyses (95% CI &−8.9 to &−0.6) and 6.4 points lower in matched–set fixed–effects analyses (95% CI &−10.7 to &−2.1). Among reviews with assessable ROBIS ratings, 75.0% of AI-assisted reviews and 65.6% of comparators were rated low risk (adjusted difference +17.8 percentage points; 95% CI 2.7 to 33.0). Among AI-assisted reviews, model version or date was reported in 42.9%, prompts or parameters in 55.8%, and data-governance or ethics considerations in 9.1%. Conclusions: Reviews reporting AI assistance had lower methodological–adherence scores and had less complete reporting, despite more favorable risk–of–bias ratings. These findings provide an early warning that AI–assisted systematic reviews may require stronger safeguards, human verification, and transparency to support trust.

items.title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
items.summary: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. items.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness

items.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least 1.93times as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality 1.62times sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd

items.abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

items.summary: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. items.abstract: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables \(32\times\) and even effective \(64\times\) compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At \(1024\times1024\) resolution, our model delivers a \(20\times\) speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

items.title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module
items.summary: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by…
items.abstract: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.

items.abstract: China's oncology drug development ecosystem has shifted from rapid pipeline expansion toward clinical value-driven innovation. We review regulatory reform and the 2015 to 2025 evolution of clinical development across small molecules, mAbs, multispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and cell and gene therapies. China's disease burden and enrollment capacity have enabled globally relevant advances in EGFR-mutant lung cancer, gastrointestinal malignancies, hepatocellular carcinoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and CLDN18.2-directed therapies. We highlight persistent challenges in target and modality convergence, biomarker definition, therapeutic window optimization, manufacturing consistency, and globally interpretable evidence generation and discuss how artificial intelligence may connect target discovery, drug design, and clinical trial optimization more efficiently. Significance China has become a major source of oncology trials and modality innovation, but scale alone will not ensure global impact. This review links regulatory reform, disease-specific opportunity, target biology, therapeutic format, and evidence quality across a decade of solid tumor development. It defines the conditions under which China-originated programs can generate globally practice-changing evidence. See related article by Shi, p. XX .

items.abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

items.abstract: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.

items.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.

items.abstract: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

items.abstract: Task-based fMRI of the cervical spinal cord is limited by physiological noise and small sample sizes. The primary objective of this study was to examine whether a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based denoising framework can improve the detection of task-dependent functional connectivity between cervical spinal segments using generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis. An open dataset of 26 healthy adults performing a hand-grasp task with alternating right- and left-hand blocks during 3 T fMRI was analyzed. A CNN with Inception V3 transfer learning (91.0% slice-level and 89.2% block-level accuracy) was trained to classify grasp versus rest, and the trained model was then utilized to derive denoised time series from masks of the spinal segments C5-C8. A gPPI model with a C6 ventral horn seed was evaluated using FDR correction and permutation testing (n = 1000). C6 showed positive task-dependent connectivity with C7 (β = 0.72, p = 0.003) and C8 (β = 0.58, p = 0.018), and negative connectivity with C5 (β = -0.31, p = 0.041), which is broadly consistent with the organization of the cervical myotomes. The C6-C5 effect was marginal and was not detected when conventional time series were used (p = 0.21), and therefore it requires replication. Grad-CAM maps aligned with ventral horn motor pools (Dice = 0.89 at C7). These results suggest that deep learning-based denoising may increase the sensitivity of spinal cord fMRI to segmental connectivity, although validation in larger cohorts is needed.

items.abstract: Radiation dose in medical imaging has been quantified through measurable metrics such as computed tomography dose index volume (CTDIvol), dose length product (DLP), kerma area product, kerma at reference point etc. They are benchmarked through diagnostic reference levels (DRLs); and communicated in terms of effective dose and population-based risk estimates. None of these tools was designed to describe the dose, the reference standard, or the risk applicable to the individual patient. In every other domain of medicine where a potentially harmful agent accompanies a beneficial clinical intervention, from contrast nephrotoxicity in CT imaging to anesthetic risk in surgery, the field has moved beyond population metrics to individualized measurement and individual clinical decision-making. Radiation protection in medical imaging has not yet made this transition. This paper resolves several open questions on cumulative dose that have long been used to justify inaction. It argues that the transition is now technically achievable, that the barriers to it are primarily architectural, regulatory, and cultural rather than physical or computational, and that artificial intelligence and emerging imaging technologies provide the enabling infrastructure to complete it. We describe the three-tier structure of barriers to individual dose tracking: technical, institutional and regulatory, and cultural; and propose the elements of a system that would place the individual patient's cumulative radiation dose record where it belongs: in their medical record, alongside their medication list, visible at the point of every subsequent clinical imaging decision.

items.abstract: Neuro-oncology biomarkers allow probing tissues beyond anatomical or relaxation contrast. However, new techniques are needed to achieve mechanistic elucidation and effective therapeutic interventions. Quantitative MRI techniques, such as T 1 , T 2 , diffusion, and perfusion imaging, provide insights into tumor biology, infiltration, microstructure, and hemodynamics, and have been implemented clinically, but are limited in probing cellular and molecular changes. Saturation transfer (ST) MRI methods, including magnetization transfer contrast (MTC) and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), exhibit enhanced sensitivity to semisolid macromolecular content, mobile proteins, tissue metabolites, and acidosis. Despite these advantages, ST-MRI techniques typically have been qualitative or semi-quantitative, time-consuming, and impractical for clinical implementation. However, emerging ST-MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) represents a significant analytical advancement by integrating RF saturation preparation into a pseudo-randomized MRF acquisition framework with a deep learning-based reconstruction. This approach enables simultaneous, clinically realistic, quantitative mapping of bulk water relaxation properties (e.g., T 1 and T 2 ), semisolid macromolecular parameters, and exchangeable solute dynamics (e.g., pool size ratios and exchange rates). We provide a comprehensive background, methodological principles, and evolving clinical applications of ST-MRF in neuro-oncology. We explore current advancements, strengths, limitations, and future possibilities for clinical translation into neuro-oncology workflows, including tumor characterization, treatment response monitoring, infiltration mapping, and biomarker development.

items.abstract: Background Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an inherited vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in multiple organs. Although brain MRI screening is recommended in all patients with HHT, in many centers, this may be difficult to implement due to organizational constraints. The aim of this study was to develop a machine learning model to predict the presence of bAVMs and other cerebrovascular malformations in patients with HHT, with the goal of supporting risk stratification in centers where genotype information is already available and identifying patients who may benefit from closer and more conservative surveillance. Methods All patients with confirmed diagnosis of HHT, complete genetic work-up, and radiological screening (2018-2026) were included for the analysis. Two end points were defined: probability of detecting bAVMs, and probability of detecting any cerebrovascular findings. Analysis was performed using Python and R. Results A total of 142 patients with confirmed HHT (meeting ≥ 3 Curaçao criteria) were included. For bAVM prediction, both models showed good discrimination, with an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.73-0.94) for Logistic Regression (LR) and 0.85 (95% CI: 0.74-0.96) for Random Forest (RF). Despite the slightly higher AUC, RF showed lower specificity, PPV, and F1 score, higher sensitivity (0.73 vs. 0.69) and same NPV. LR also showed better calibration, with an intercept of -0.30 (95% CI: -1.38-0.78) and slope of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.34-1.40), compared with 1.39 (95% CI: -0.46-3.23) and 2.39 (95% CI: 0.64-4.15), respectively, for RF. In contrast, models predicting overall cerebrovascular malformations showed limited discrimination and poor calibration with both LR and RF. For bAVM prediction, LR identified deletion mutations, ENG, family history, ACVRL1, and truncated variants as the most influential features, while RF SHAP analysis highlighted ACVRL1, ENG, age, pulmonary AVMs, and family history. Conclusion Effective risk stratification was achieved by the phenotype-specific bAVM model, supporting its potential applicability. Upon external validation this tool may enable an efficient allocation of screening strategies.

items.abstract: Objectives To develop TotalSpineSeg, a robust tool for vertebrae and intervertebral disc instance segmentation, along with spinal cord and spinal canal segmentation, capable of processing any 3D medical image regardless of contrast, resolution, or field of view, while overcoming fusion and fragmentation errors common in standard segmentation. Materials and methods A two-stage cascaded deep learning model was trained on 1404 MRIs. To explicitly prevent errors where adjacent vertebrae merge or a single vertebra splits, the architecture employs a novel "odd/even" representation. The second stage is conditioned on an odd-intervertebral disc mask from the first stage to assign distinct semantic classes to alternating vertebrae, enforcing accurate separation between neighboring vertebrae. Finally, a landmark-based logic uses key anatomical points (C2-C3, C7-T1, T12-L1, and L5-S) to anchor sequential labeling, while a localizer-based strategy ensures accurate identification even in truncated, short field-of-view scans. Results Evaluation across diverse contrasts and pathologies yielded a vertebral identification rate of 96.22% on localizer MRI and generalized to CT scans with a 92.87% identification rate. For intervertebral disc instance labeling, where vertebral separation is not mandatory, both model stages attained 99% labeling accuracy with a mean positional L2 error of 1.55 mm, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Conclusion TotalSpineSeg successfully generalizes to diverse 3D medical images, overcoming variations in contrast, resolution, and field of view. The proposed topological constraints effectively eliminate vertebral fusion and fragmentation errors, delivering a state-of-the-art identification rate for both vertebrae and intervertebral discs across MRI and CT modalities. Key points Question Can a topology-constrained framework overcome heterogeneous contrasts and resolution limits, including localizers, to ensure robust, automated vertebral and disc labeling? Findings TotalSpineSeg achieved a high identification rate across diverse contrasts, localizers, and CT, surpassing state-of-the-art methods by eliminating fusion and fragmentation errors. Clinical relevance TotalSpineSeg enables fully automated biomarker extraction from clinical scans, allowing precise assessment of stenosis, lesions, and atrophy against normative ranges.

items.abstract: Endolymphatic hydrops MRI is used for the diagnostic evaluation of patients with primary or secondary endolymphatic hydrops. Delayed intravenous post-Gd 3-dimensional fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (3D-FLAIR) and 3-dimensional real inversion recovery (3D-real IR) sequences are the most widely applied techniques, because they exploit subtle Gd-related signal differences between perilymph and endolymph. Yet image quality and diagnostic confidence depend on protocol design, and variation persists between institutions, scanners, and vendors. This educational review provides a visually oriented, practical framework for optimising endolymphatic hydrops MRI, focusing on three core determinants: acquisition parameters, post-processing strategies, and contrast-agent selection. The physical principles underlying key sequence-parameter choices are explained, including the use of long echo trains to maximise acquisition efficiency, prolonged repetition times to enhance the perilymphatic signal, and inversion times tailored to the selected repetition time to achieve effective suppression of the endolymphatic signal. Representative graphs and imaging examples illustrate how protocol modifications influence contrast and diagnostic performance. The review further discusses post-processing approaches and emerging artificial intelligence-based techniques, including deep learning reconstruction, as tools to improve image quality, shorten scan time, or support higher spatial resolution. Finally, the role of gadolinium-based contrast agents, scan delay, and clinical protocol design is also addressed. Four-hour delayed intravenous imaging remains the current standard, although sequence-specific timing, single- or two-step protocols, and half-dose high-relaxivity agents may offer opportunities for tailored imaging, reduced Gd exposure, and improved sustainability. By linking sequence principles to practical protocol choices, this review aims to support reproducible, high-quality hydrops MRI across clinical settings. KEY POINTS: Question Optimisation and standardisation of 3D-FLAIR and 3D-real IR protocols are essential for accurate, reproducible assessment of endolymphatic hydrops across institutions, scanner platforms, and vendors. Findings Use TE 500-700 ms and a long echo train for efficiency/background suppression, TR ~ 16,000 ms to enhance perilymph, and TI 2400-3000 ms to suppress endolymph. Critical relevance statement Emerging deep-learning reconstruction techniques may shorten acquisition times or improve spatial resolution, while half-dose, high-relaxivity GBCAs may provide hydrops visualisation comparable to higher-dose conventional contrast protocols.

items.abstract: This retrospective single-center study evaluated segment-level agreement between experienced cardiac radiologists and a research AI platform for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Asymptomatic individuals undergoing CCTA at a health screening center were studied, excluding those with prior revascularization, coronary anomaly, or total occlusion. Stenosis grade and plaque composition were independently assessed by the AI platform and two cardiac radiologists at the segment level, with disagreements between the two radiologists resolved by consensus. Agreement was evaluated using Cohen's κ, quadratic weighted κ for ordinal grading, observed agreement, and positive and negative agreement for dichotomized significant stenosis. The cohort comprised 172 participants and 2,582 segments. Significant stenosis was uncommon (18/2,582, 0.7%), with moderate agreement (κ = 0.412; observed agreement 98.5%; positive agreement 0.418; negative agreement 0.992). Agreement was fair for ordinal stenosis grade (κ = 0.397; quadratic weighted κ = 0.573; observed agreement 84.0%) and plaque composition (κ = 0.330; observed agreement 81.8%). Stenosis-grade agreement was lower in plaque-containing than plaque-free segments, an exploratory finding given marked differences in subgroup size and prevalence. Myocardial bridging and image quality were not major descriptive determinants of discordance. In this low-prevalence cohort, AI-based CCTA analysis showed high negative agreement for radiologist-defined significant stenosis but limited concordance for grading and plaque characterization. Reflecting low prevalence and few positive cases, the findings do not establish independent rule-out performance but support prospective evaluation of AI as an expert-supervised pre-reading or triage adjunct, with positive, ambiguous, or plaque-containing findings requiring expert review.

items.abstract: Objectives This systematic review aims to evaluate the techniques and reported patterns of heatmap-based visual explanations in deep learning (DL) systems for dental radiographic classification tasks. Methods A literature search following PRISMA guidelines was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore Library, Oria.no and Google Scholar to retrieve studies using DL for dental classification tasks. Only articles with a visual explanation (heatmap) were selected. Risk of bias assessment was done with QUADAS-2, PROBAST-AI and CEBM. The heatmap technique, reasons for inclusion, explanations provided and patterns were analysed. Results In the 136 studies reviewed, Grad-CAM was the most commonly used technique. The predominant reason for using visual explanations was to understand the decision-making process of the DL model. Some heatmaps reflect established radiographic criteria, while others exhibit unique, label-dependent patterns that sometimes emphasise irrelevant areas. Cropping to the region of interest influences visual explanations. Conclusions Visual explanations seem clinically plausible to domain experts when aligned with domain knowledge, but clinical plausibility does not equal technical faithfulness. Formal faithfulness testing was rarely performed among the included studies. Therefore, explanations should not be assumed to accurately represent the model's underlying reasoning. Limitations include the evaluation of studies not primarily designed for visual explanation assessment. No funding was received for this review. Authors declare no competing interests. Advances in knowledge Visual explanations, while clinically plausible when aligned with domain knowledge, remain insufficiently validated and should not be assumed to faithfully represent model reasoning. An implausible explanation does not necessarily indicate model failure. Domain/task-specific evaluation metrics for explainable AI in dentomaxillofacial radiology are needed.
