items.abstract: Objectives Although the precise mechanism underlying activation of Spo0A needs to be clarified to fully understand C. perfringens sporulation, the molecules directly interacting with Spo0A have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to identify proteins interacting with Spo0A during C. perfringens sporulation by a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay. Methods Prey libraries constructed using the genomes of C. perfringens SM101 and str. 13 and a bait plasmid encoding the receiver domain of Spo0A in C. perfringens SM101 were used for Y2H assay. The deletion mutant and its complemented strain were constructed by homologous recombination. Phenotypic analyses included measurements of bacterial growth, sporulation efficiency, cell morphology, mRNA expression of sporulation-related genes, and the amount of phosphorylated Spo0A. Potential protein interactions were evaluated using AlphaFold 3. Results Y2H screening identified CPR0186, a hypothetical protein in C. perfringens SM101, as a Spo0A-interacting candidate, and AlphaFold 3 modeling supported the possibility of the direct interaction with the receiver domain of Spo0A. The cpr0186-null mutant exhibited growth comparable to that of the wild-type strain, but showed significantly reduced sporulation. The mutant also showed significantly decreased mRNA expression of spo0A, sigF, sigE, sigG, and sigK. No apparent difference in the ratio of Spo0A∼P to unphosphorylated Spo0A was observed among the strains under the conditions tested. Conclusion cpr0186 promotes sporulation in C. perfringens SM101 and is suggested to contribute to the expression of Spo0A-regulated genes. CPR0186 may interact directly with Spo0A although the functional significance of this interaction remains to be determined.

items.abstract: Snakebite envenoming remains a major public health problem in Latin America. Although antivenoms are produced by many Latin American manufacturers, their use in accidents involving heterologous snake species or from different geographic areas requires preclinical testing, typically conducted in experimental animals. Here, we assessed whether toxin-centered in silico analyses can predict antivenom efficacy by evaluating the performance of the Instituto Butantan Bothrops antivenom against venoms from medically relevant Ecuadorian Bothrops asper, B. atrox, and B. bilineatus. We combined transcriptome-guided proteomics, toxin phylogeny, AlphaFold-based structural modeling, and DiscoTope epitope mapping to compare Ecuadorian venom toxins with those in the immunization mixture used for antivenom production. Although toxin abundance and composition varied among venoms, most Ecuadorian toxins had close orthologs in the immunization mixture, and most predicted epitope residues were conserved or showed conservative substitutions, suggesting broad antibody recognition. Divergent toxins, particularly some PLA 2 s, PI-class SVMPs, SVSPs, and CTLs, showed non-conservative substitutions that could reduce antibody binding. Experimental validation supported these predictions: ELISA and Western blotting showed strong antivenom reactivity, while in vivo assays demonstrated complete neutralization of lethality and hemorrhagic activity, with partial limitations against B. asper myotoxicity and the defibrinogenating activity induced by B. asper and B. atrox. These findings indicate that epitope-focused in silico approaches can support antivenom efficacy assessment and guide antivenom improvement while reducing reliance on animal testing. Moreover, we demonstrated that the Instituto Butantan Bothrops antivenom effectively neutralizes the lethality and specific toxic activities of important medically relevant venoms from Bothrops snakes in Ecuador.

items.abstract: Missense variants in glycan-related genes (glycogenes) underlie many congenital disorders of glycosylation and related conditions, yet a large fraction remain classified as variants of uncertain significance. Because glycogenes often show low evolutionary conservation, conventional sequence-based predictors are frequently uninformative, making structure-based interpretation particularly valuable. This review examines how structure-based and glycosylation-aware approaches can improve the interpretation of glycogene variants. Advances in protein structure prediction, notably AlphaFold, now allow variant-induced structural perturbations to be assessed proteome-wide using structure-derived features such as solvent accessibility, thermodynamic stability (ΔΔG), and local model confidence (pLDDT). Such structural features can be combined to predict the impact of glycogene variants, as exemplified by VarMeter and VarMeter2, which have successfully identified pathogenic missense variants of arylsulfatase L (ARSL) and N-sulfoglucosamine sulfohydrolase (SGSH) in patients with undiagnosed disease. Despite the progress in these tools, there remain challenges especially relevant to glycobiology, including the limited accuracy of current ΔΔG predictors, the distinct behavior of gain-of-function and stabilizing variants, the need for proteome-scale computation, and the critical but still underexplored contribution of protein glycosylation to structural stability. We argue that incorporating glycosylation into structural energetics is a key next step toward more accurate, glyco-aware variant interpretation.

items.abstract: Introduction Nanoparticle drug delivery systems (NP DDS) have transformed therapeutic delivery by improving drug stability, extending circulation time, and enabling targeted biodistribution. However, clinical translation remains limited by protein corona formation, immune recognition, and accelerated blood clearance following repeated administration. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has been the gold-standard antifouling material for decades, but emerging anti-PEG immune responses have driven the search for alternative stealth technologies. Areas covered Zwitterionic peptides (ZIPs) have emerged as a promising class of antifouling materials because they combine the hydration-mediated stealth properties of zwitterionic polymers with the molecular precision and programmability of peptide synthesis. Here, ZIP applications in drug delivery were reviewed using the Web of Science database from 2014-2026, focusing on reducing and controlling the protein corona, recent advances in ZIP-based drug delivery, and the potential of high-throughput screening platforms and machine learning-guided ZIP design. Recent studies suggest that biological interactions of ZIP-functionalized NPs are governed primarily by charge motifs rather than precise sequences, creating new opportunities for material design. Expert opinion This observation motivates developing semi-randomized ZIPs (srZIPs) that preserve charge organization while introducing sequence diversity. By maintaining key physicochemical and biological properties while diversifying composition, srZIPs may reduce immune recognition without sacrificing antifouling function.

items.abstract: Objectives To synthesize evidence on artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled postoperative pain assessment and prediction, opioid-related risk prediction, patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) monitoring, and implementation considerations in pediatric surgical care. Design A systematic review with narrative synthesis of evidence concerning AI applications in pediatric postoperative pain management and opioid stewardship. Data sources Biomedical, nursing, engineering, computer science, trial-registry, Google Scholar, and citation sources were systematically searched through March 2026. Review/analysis methods Eligible studies evaluated AI, machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, multimodal sensing, or AI-enabled tools in pediatric surgical or postoperative populations. A single reviewer performed study selection, data extraction, and methodological appraisal, with consultation from an external subject-matter expert. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed using design-appropriate appraisal tools. Findings were narratively synthesized because clinical and methodological heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results Of 198 identified records, 137 were screened, and 20 full-text reports were assessed. Eleven studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, alongside one companion dataset report. Applications included automated pain assessment, home-based pain monitoring, prolonged opioid-use prediction, and prediction of pain or adverse effects during PCA. Most studies evaluated facial expressions using computer vision or multimodal combinations of physiological, video, and audio data. Reported performance varied substantially, with validation predominantly limited to internal datasets. No randomized trial or controlled clinical-impact study demonstrated reductions in pain intensity, opioid exposure or prescribing, adverse events, readmissions, or length of stay attributable to AI-guided care. Conclusions AI-enabled tools show potential to support pediatric postoperative pain assessment and opioid-related risk stratification. However, current evidence is insufficient to justify routine clinical implementation. External validation, prospective clinical evaluation, fairness assessment, and workflow-integrated effectiveness studies are needed. Nursing practice implications AI-enabled assessment and prediction tools may complement pediatric nurses' clinical assessment, pain monitoring, opioid-related risk identification, patient and family education, and timely escalation of care. Nevertheless, their use should remain supplementary to professional nursing judgment until clinical effectiveness, safety, and generalizability are established.

items.abstract: Background Voice disorders can substantially impair communication and quality of life, creating a need for reliable, non-invasive, and reproducible approaches for automated voice assessment. Conventional acoustic features such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) have been widely used for voice-disorder classification, but their ability to represent the frequency selectivity and nonlinear characteristics of human auditory processing may be limited. Auditory-inspired representations derived from cochlear modeling may provide complementary information for distinguishing pathological voice patterns. Objectives This study investigates the effectiveness of three acoustic representations, namely Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), Gammatone Filterbank Cepstral Coefficients (GTFCC), and Gammachirp Filterbank Cepstral Coefficients (GCFCC), in combination with different convolutional neural network architectures for multiclass voice-disorder classification. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluating these representations under a strict speaker-independent validation protocol designed to reduce the risk of speaker leakage. Methods Experiments were conducted using a subset of the Saarbrücken Voice Database (SVD) comprising 3022 recordings from 262 speakers, representing seven diagnostic categories: healthy voice, functional dysphonia, laryngitis, leukoplakia, psychogenic dysphonia, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, and spasmodic dysphonia. All recordings were converted to mono, resampled to 16 kHz, band-pass filtered between 80 Hz and 8 kHz, amplitude-normalized, and temporally standardized to 300 frames using truncation or zero-padding. Three feature representations were extracted: MFCC, GTFCC based on an ERB-spaced Gammatone filterbank, and GCFCC based on Gammachirp auditory filtering. Each representation comprised 13 cepstral coefficients together with their first- and second-order temporal derivatives, resulting in 39 × 300 time-frequency feature maps. These representations were evaluated using a custom convolutional neural network, VGG16-BN, and ResNet-50. A speaker-independent five-fold cross-validation strategy was employed. All recordings from the same speaker were assigned to a single fold and remained within a single partition throughout the evaluation. Within each fold, data augmentation and class balancing were applied exclusively to the training partition, while validation and test recordings remained unaltered. The augmented training data were generated using controlled Gaussian-noise injection and pitch shifting, followed by targeted augmentation of underrepresented classes. Classification performance was assessed using accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score, together with 95% confidence intervals and fold-level variability. Statistical comparisons between feature representations were performed using paired t tests with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. Results Across the evaluated architectures, the cochlear-inspired representations generally provided higher classification performance than conventional MFCCs, with GCFCC yielding the strongest overall performance. The best-performing configuration was ResNet-50 combined with GCFCC, achieving a mean accuracy of 94.77% (95% CI: 94.36 to 95.18%), with fold-wise accuracies ranging from 94.43% to 95.17%. The corresponding macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score were 94.46% (95% CI: 93.81 to 95.10%), 94.94% (95% CI: 94.35 to 95.53%), and 94.67% (95% CI: 94.31 to 95.03%), respectively. The coefficient of variation for accuracy was 0.35%, indicating relatively low inter-fold variability under the speaker-independent evaluation protocol. Statistical analysis further supported the advantage of GCFCC over GTFCC and MFCC for accuracy across the evaluated architectures, although not all differences in macro-averaged F1-score reached statistical significance after multiple-comparison correction. Conclusions The findings indicate that cochlear-inspired cepstral representations, particularly GCFCC, can provide useful acoustic information for multiclass voice-disorder classification when combined with deep residual learning. The strict speaker-independent evaluation and training-only augmentation provide a conservative estimate of performance within the evaluated SVD subset. However, the results should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical diagnostic capability. External validation on independent databases, additional speaking conditions and languages, connected speech, and prospective clinical cohorts is required to determine the generalizability and clinical utility of the proposed framework.

items.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy faces a critical clinical hurdle: cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Current CRS management strategies have limited selectivity and may interfere with CAR-T cell antitumor activity, highlighting the need for more targeted and precisely controllable interventions. Nanoengineering offers a promising approach to address these limitations by enabling the spatiotemporally controlled monitoring and modulation of inflammatory responses, with the potential to mitigate excessive cytokine release while preserving CAR-T cell therapeutic efficacy, driving a paradigm shift toward programmable, proactive immune regulation. This review systematically examines nanointervention strategies for mitigating CAR-T-induced CRS, including molecular monitoring, cytokine clearance, targeted delivery, stimulus-responsive systems, biomimetic designs, and genetic reprogramming. These approaches enable precise intervention across multiple stages-from early inflammation detection and localized neutralization to source-level cellular engineering. Finally, we discuss challenges in biosafety, clinical translation, and the potential of artificial intelligence-driven predictive platforms. Nanotechnology offers a transformative pathway to redefine CRS from an unpredictable complication into a manageable therapeutic window, paving the way for safer next-generation cellular immunotherapies.

items.abstract: Background Heart failure is classically divided into two subtypes based on the ejection fraction (EF): HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), each with varying risk mitigation strategies. Electrocardiogram-based artificial intelligence (AI) may facilitate HF subtype-specific risk prediction, to enable tailored prevention. Methods and results Based on a previously validated HF prediction architecture, we developed an ECG-based AI model to predict 10-year risk of incident HFrEF (LVEF <50%) versus HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%) (Electrocardiogram to Heart Failure Subtype, "ECG2HF-Subtype"). ECG2HF-Subtype was developed in 98,190 individuals in Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), and validated in three test sets: MGH, Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH), and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), among individuals without prior HF. HF was identified using a validated natural language processing model, and subtypes were classified by LVEF proximate to incident HF. Discrimination was quantified using time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP), with comparisons to age and sex, and a multinomial logistic regression classifier including PREVENT-HF variables. In aggregate, models were evaluated in MGH (n=16,739, age 56±17, 54% women), BWH (n=75,195, 56±16, 59%) and BIDMC (n=30,133, 56±17, 54%). ECG2HF-Subtype consistently discriminated incident HFrEF (MGH 10-year AUROC 0.89 [0.86-0.91], 10-year AP: 0.11 [95%CI 0.09-0.15], cumulative incidence 1.73%; BWH: 0.88 [0.87-0.89], 0.13 [0.11-0.14], 2.23% BIDMC: 0.88 [0.86-0.89], 0.14 [0.12-0.17], 2.19%) and HFpEF events (MGH 10-year AUROC 0.83 [0.81-0.85], 10-year AP: 0.10 [95% CI 0.09-0.13], cumulative incidence 3.17%; BWH: 0.79 [0.77-0.80], 0.06 [0.06-0.07], 2.75%), BIDMC: 0.81 [0.80-0.82], 0.10 [0.09-0.12], 3.49%), with consistently greater AUROC versus age and sex. When compared to PREVENT-HF variables, ECG2HF-Subtypes had favorable discrimination of HFrEF (e.g., 10-year AUROC in MGH+BWH 0.86 [0.84-0.88] vs. 0.78 [0.76-0.80]), and modestly lower for HFpEF (10-year AUROC in MGH+BWH 0.78 [0.76-0.80] vs. 0.81 [0.79-0.82]). Conclusions By predicting risk of HFpEF and HFrEF, AI-enabled ECG analysis may enable targeted prevention to reduce HF-related morbidity.

items.abstract: Sustained adherence to intraocular pressure-lowering medications is essential for preventing progressive visual loss in patients with glaucoma on pharmacotherapy. However, adherence remains suboptimal across patient populations as the result of cognitive, behavioural, physical, and socioeconomic barriers. Recent advances in digital health have introduced smartphone-based adherence supports intended to reinforce glaucoma medication routines, improve treatment organization, and support self-management. This narrative review synthesises evidence examining smartphone-based reminder applications and related digital adherence supports in glaucoma care, with attention to usability, patient experience, behavioural determinants, and clinical feasibility. Preliminary studies have reported improvements in short-term self-reported adherence and glaucoma-specific quality of life, particularly among patients with low baseline adherence. However, reminder-based interventions may provide only temporary benefit if they do not address broader structural, behavioural, and situational barriers to adherence. Current evidence remains limited by short follow-up durations, reliance on self-reported adherence measures, and limited evaluation of long-term clinical outcomes such as intraocular pressure stability and visual field preservation. Digital adherence tools may therefore be most effective when integrated alongside broader behavioural and relationship-based support strategies, including patient education, clinician communication, and caregiver involvement. Emerging technologies such as automated messaging systems and artificial intelligence-assisted tools may represent future directions for adherence support, although evidence in glaucoma remains limited. Further research is required to establish personalised, durable, and equitable adherence support frameworks in glaucoma care.

items.abstract: High-throughput technologies now make it possible to simultaneously generate genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data. Spatial and single-cell platforms, in turn, provide cellular and spatial information in greater detail. Relying on a single omics method captures only a fraction of this complexity and often overlooks interactions across different layers. Despite these advances, clinical applications remain limited. This review examines integration strategies, along with their applications in various diseases, and the machine learning methods used to implement them. Rather than focusing solely on predictive performance, the aim is to support biological reasoning by formulating testable hypotheses, drawing causal inferences, and gaining insights that can guide clinical decisions. A reanalysis of a publicly available chronic lymphocytic leukemia dataset revealed that one data type was missing in approximately one-third of patients. When early and intermediate integration were combined with simple zero imputation, agreement dropped to chance and near-chance levels. In contrast, late integration, which does not require data imputation, was largely unaffected by this issue. This demonstrates that findings regarding integration strategies cannot be considered in isolation from how missing data are handled. The review also covers approaches that directly address missing data. Major barriers to clinical application include confounding batch effects, unreliable feature attribution when features are correlated, and deficiencies in clinical quality assurance. This review proposes four criteria to help identify models that not only ensure statistical validity but also genuinely support biological reasoning: mechanistic specificity, causal grounding, failure transparency, and decision relevance.

items.abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

items.title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
items.summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements,…
items.abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.

items.title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
items.summary: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate…
items.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

items.title: Energy-Tweedie: Score meets Score, Energy meets Energy
items.summary: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example. We derive the Energy-Tweedie identity: when the denoising…
items.abstract: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example. We derive the Energy-Tweedie identity: when the denoising posterior is viewed through the lens of scoring rules, the path derivative of a kernel scoring rule defined by the noise potential recovers the Stein score of the noisy marginal. Thus, the familiar correspondence between Gaussian noise, posterior means, squared loss, and Tweedie's formula is lifted to a distributional correspondence between Gibbs noise distributions, full posterior laws, kernel scoring rules, and the Energy-Tweedie identity, which gives a Tweedie-style relation for each noise potential. Among its consequences, this identity gives a posterior-samples-to-score route to score estimation, yields a principled criterion for estimating unknown noise parameters, and enables diffusion-style sampling along user-chosen paths through the noise-parameter space, supplying the score-based perspective on recent generative methods trained with scoring rules.

items.title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding…
items.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. items.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

items.title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
items.summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to…
items.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

items.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
items.summary: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol…
items.abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

items.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
items.summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that…
items.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.

items.abstract: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver--judge--repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an additional set of easier tasks to support evaluation of smaller models.

items.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

items.abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.

items.abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

items.title: Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
items.summary: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose…
items.abstract: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model-harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

items.title: OmniLatent: Unified Latent for 3D Part Modeling
items.summary: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns…
items.abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.

items.title: Video-Coder: Reinforcing Agentic Coding for Video Generation
items.summary: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to…
items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code

items.title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
items.summary: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and…
items.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. Homepage: https://wsp-scope.github.io/ GitHub: https://github.com/WSP-Scope/WSP-Scope-Project

items.title: SIRIS: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation Errors Matter in AI-Driven Systems Research
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected. We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart, judging from their systems understanding when a limitation…
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected. We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart, judging from their systems understanding when a limitation invalidates the simulator's recommendation. By perturbing a simulator, Siris constructs workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation, and simulator recommendation. The perturbation changes predictions on both workloads, yet a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only one. Evaluating thirteen frontier LLMs on LLM serving design problems, we find that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice, and even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations. Self-correction through a review turn helps these models restore valid choices but introduces new errors in several others. These findings motivate evaluating systems understanding through design decisions under imperfect simulators.

items.title: Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence
items.summary: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder…
items.abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.

items.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
items.summary: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for…
items.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

items.title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
items.summary: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one…
items.abstract: Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

items.title: Utilising digital technologies for mycetoma management: A comprehensive review of advances and opportunities.
items.summary: Mycetoma is a neglected tropical disease characterised by chronic, destructive infections of subcutaneous tissues, predominantly affecting populations in endemic regions with limited healthcare resources. Delayed diagnosis, limited treatment options, and restricted access to specialised healthcare contribute to substantial morbidity, disability, and socioeconomic burden. Digital technologies offer promising…
items.abstract: Mycetoma is a neglected tropical disease characterised by chronic, destructive infections of subcutaneous tissues, predominantly affecting populations in endemic regions with limited healthcare resources. Delayed diagnosis, limited treatment options, and restricted access to specialised healthcare contribute to substantial morbidity, disability, and socioeconomic burden. Digital technologies offer promising opportunities to address these challenges and improve mycetoma care. Artificial intelligence (AI) can support early detection and diagnostic accuracy through the analysis of clinical images, radiological findings, and patient data. Telemedicine can facilitate remote specialist consultations and follow-up, particularly in rural and underserved communities, while electronic health records enable systematic data collection, disease surveillance, and monitoring of treatment outcomes. Mobile health applications can improve patient education, symptom monitoring, and treatment adherence, whereas computational drug discovery may accelerate the identification of potential therapeutic agents. Furthermore, digital platforms can strengthen international research collaborations, knowledge exchange, and capacity building. However, implementing these technologies in endemic regions faces significant barriers, including inadequate digital infrastructure, limited internet connectivity, insufficient digital literacy, data privacy concerns, and ethical challenges related to informed consent, data ownership, and algorithmic decision-making. Addressing these barriers requires investment in infrastructure, appropriate regulatory frameworks, stakeholder collaboration, and context-specific capacity-building initiatives. Integrating digital health solutions into national healthcare strategies could support sustainable and equitable improvements in mycetoma management. This review highlights the potential applications, opportunities, and challenges of digital technologies in mycetoma care and emphasises the need for inclusive, locally adapted approaches to enhance early diagnosis, treatment outcomes, research, and health equity in endemic communities.

items.abstract: Diethyl phthalate (DEP) is a ubiquitous environmental endocrine-disrupting chemical to which human populations are widely exposed. Increasing evidence links DEP to the malignant progression of solid tumors; however, the key molecular networks and experimentally validated mechanisms underlying DEP-enhanced invasion in gastric cancer (GC) remain largely undefined. Four transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus were integrated to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), followed by weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to determine tumor-associated key modules. Potential DEP targets were predicted using multiple databases and intersected with-related DEGs and key module genes to define core candidate genes. Functional enrichment and network analyses were then performed. Subsequently, a multi-model ensemble machine learning framework combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based interpretability was applied to prioritize candidate genes. Molecular docking was used to evaluate the potential binding affinity between DEP and key target proteins. Finally, the effects of DEP on oxidative stress, migration and invasion, cytoskeletal remodeling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) were experimentally validated in AGS and HGC-27 cells. Thirteen core candidate genes were identified. Functional enrichment analyses primarily implicated lysosomal proteolysis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and chromatin remodeling and epigenetic regulation. Among the evaluated machine learning models, the gradient boosting machine (GBM) model demonstrated the best overall diagnostic performance. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis of an additional random forest model highlighted CTSB, PLAU, ALDH3A1, ATAD2, and CBX7 as influential features for GC classification. Molecular docking predicted potential interactions between DEP and these candidate proteins. In vitro experiments demonstrated that DEP exposure increased intracellular reactive oxygen species levels and promoted cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in AGS and HGC-27 cells. These effects were accompanied by filamentous actin (F-actin) reorganization, increased RhoA and MLC1 expression, decreased E-cadherin expression, and increased N-cadherin and vimentin expression, consistent with EMT-related alterations. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that DEP exposure enhances invasion-related malignant phenotypes in gastric cancer cells and identify candidate molecular targets potentially associated with GC progression. Although network toxicology, machine learning, and molecular docking provide complementary evidence for target prioritization, further functional studies are required to determine whether these candidate targets directly mediate DEP-induced cellular effects.

Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. items.abstract: The quantitative measurement of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence images of cells remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. Here, we present MitoDecode, a deep learning network that automatically assesses type and severity of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence microscopy images. MitoDecode eliminates the need for mitochondrial segmentation, is parameter-free, and operates across both diffraction-limited and super-resolution optical imaging modalities. It assigns a phenotypic probability profile for each individual cell, indicating both type and severity of phenotypic stress. The readout thus enables comparisons between different stressors and provides clues for underlying mechanisms. Furthermore, the method captures phenotypic shifts continuously across treatment doses, revealing subtle variations that would otherwise be missed. We demonstrate MitoDecode’s adaptability across diverse cell types, imaging modalities, and stress conditions, and show that it can reliably detect mitochondrial phenotypes, even when stressors target non-mitochondrial pathways. We validate the reliability of the model with biochemical assays, showcase its utility for phenotypic stress profiling of drug treatments, and envisage its application for early-stage disease detection, drug discovery, and mechanistic lead generation.

items.abstract: Olfaction-based biosensors stand to have profound impacts in fields such as medical diagnostics, national security, and drug discovery. A promising mode of vapor phase biodetection mimics volatile organic compound-olfactory receptor (VOC-OR) interactions with target-specific protein or peptide probes; however, lack of experimental coverage remains a core bottleneck. Current computational approaches aim to improve prediction of VOC-OR binding to reduce experimental burden, and current machine learning approaches fail to demonstrate a level of generalization that addresses current engineering challenges. Here, using the Molecular to Olfactory Dataset (M2OR) and Insect Olfactory Binding Protein Database (iOBPdb) datasets, data partitioning methods and their performance are evaluated on a neural network and contrastive learning framework on such VOC-OR binding datasets, varying: model training, architecture, and structure of the input data distribution. It was found that holding out certain chemical or proteomic motifs from the training data diminished model performance with a two layer neural network model. The model was able to generalize to state of the art performance (0.88 AUCROC) on every data split by applying a contrastive learning objective defined by shared molecular constituents and a stochastic sampler. This suggests the contrastive objective provides a strong inductive bias for neural networks to predict novel VOC-OR pairs. These findings highlight that model performance on pairwise biological interaction datasets can be inflated through identity leakage from constituent overlap, and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we show contrastive regularization mitigates dataset degeneracy through enforcement of compatibility in the models latent geometry that may extend to other binder target-datasets where identity leakage confounds evaluation.

items.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming of myeloid‑derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) plays a role in immunotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer (CRC). This metabolic reprogramming appears to be coordinated by oncogenic mutations (such as adenomatous polyposis coli, KRAS and TP53) through a proposed self‑reinforcing 'mutation‑metabolism‑suppression' axis. In the present review, four core metabolic pillars sustaining MDSC pathogenicity and the epimetabolic regulation that durably locks them into a suppressive state were examined. Furthermore, two emerging dimensions were highlighted: The spatial metabolic antagonism through which MDSCs may construct a metabolically hostile zone to limit the functional activity of tertiary lymphoid structures, and the remote manipulation of MDSC function by gut and intratumoral microbiota‑derived metabolites. To transcend the limitations of non‑specific myeloid depletion, immunometabolic rehabilitation is proposed as a potentially transformative framework targeting intrinsic metabolic vulnerabilities to functionally reprogram MDSCs from an immunosuppressive to a homeostatic or immunostimulatory phenotype. By integrating emerging spatial omics for precise target validation, artificial intelligence‑guided rational drug design and microbiome modulation, this paradigm provides a strategic roadmap for next‑generation precision immunotherapy, aiming to achieve durable responses across both microsatellite stable and microsatellite instability‑high CRC.

items.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded treatment options across multiple malignancies, but their clinical benefit remains constrained by heterogeneous and sometimes serious toxicities. These toxicities rarely arise from a single component; instead, they reflect the association between target biology, molecular architecture, systemic exposure, and tissue susceptibility. We first examine the structural basis of ADC toxicity by discussing the distinct contributions of the antibody-target axis, linker, payload, drug loading, and conjugation strategy to systemic exposure and tissue toxicity. We distinguish organ-selective "on-target, off-tumor" injury from target-independent toxicity and further characterize two major off-target routes: context-dependent uptake of intact ADCs through Fcγ receptor-mediated or pinocytosis-dominant pathways, and spatially distinct exposure to released payload arising from premature systemic release or localized bystander diffusion. Furthermore, we summarize a multidisciplinary management framework, ranging from prophylactic measures to graded interventions across complex scenarios such as treatment rechallenge and combination therapy. Finally, we discuss strategies to widen the therapeutic window through exposure-response-guided dosing, next-generation molecular engineering, and emerging conjugate platforms. Artificial intelligence and computational approaches may further extend safety optimization from drug design to patient stratification and real-world surveillance. By linking molecular design, spatial exposure, and clinical management, this review provides an integrated framework to improve ADC safety while preserving antitumor efficacy.

items.abstract: The preoperative prediction of clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) is crucial for the implementation of efficient prevention strategies in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Our study aimed to explore the value of habitat imaging employing virtual magnetic resonance elastography (vMRE) and continuous-time random-walk (CTRW) diffusion MRI for preoperatively predicting CR-POPF in PDAC after pancreaticoduodenectomy. vMRE reflected pancreatic stiffness, whereas CTRW-derived parameters characterized non-Gaussian water diffusion and microstructural heterogeneity. Their voxel-wise integration could identify imaging-defined phenotype reflecting complementary tissue properties. Patients with suspected PDAC who underwent pancreatic MRI were prospectively collected. Multiple-b-value diffusion-weighted imaging sequence was acquired and fitted to CTRW model. The diffusion-based tissue shear modulus (μ diff ) was calculated by calibrating the shifted apparent diffusion coefficient (sADC) with standard MR elastography (MRE). The presumed pancreatic stump was segmented into various subregions by habitat analysis employing two combinations of vMRE and CTRW parameter maps. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify the independent factors and construct the prediction models. The predictive performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve and validated using bootstrap method. A total of 183 patients were finally included, and 36 patients (19.67%) developed CR-POPF. The optimism-corrected area under the curve (AUC) of two combined models was 0.947 (95% CI, 0.898-0.987) and 0.897 (95% CI, 0.832-0.962) respectively, through bootstrap validation. Habitat analysis using vMRE and CTRW diffusion model provided complementary characterization of stiffness and diffusion heterogeneity, and exhibited great potential for the preoperative prediction of CR-POPF in PDAC after pancreaticoduodenectomy.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation can detect abnormalities, generate reports, provide visual grounding, and support dialogue but often offer limited mechanisms for inspection and follow-up. We present Transparent Radiology Assistance for Chest X-ray Explanation and Review (TRACER), a multimodal multi-agent workflow integrating CXR analysis, consultation support, and prior-report comparison with structured findings, gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) cues, report-generation steps, and execution trajectories. Evaluation included report-quality benchmarking on 2000 frontal CXRs and user studies with 60 non-radiologist participants. Experiment II used 12 cases, with one fixed report per case in both text-only and transparency-supported conditions; the latter additionally displayed structured findings, finding-specific Grad-CAM cues, and execution trajectories. Open-ended responses were scored by an independent automated judge with clinician validation on a stratified subset. Experiment III evaluated eight prior-current pairs with or without an archive-assisted comparison paragraph. The full report pipeline achieved the best values on six of eight automatic metrics. Transparency support increased Consultation Preparation Quality from 2.133 ± 1.302 to 3.142 ± 1.154 (odds ratio 6.76, 95% confidence interval 3.92-11.67; P<0.001 ). Archive assistance improved difference identification from 0.642±0.338 to 0.833±0.285 (odds ratio 4.16, 95% confidence interval 2.33-7.42; P<0.001 ) and reduced mean completion time from 108.825 to 74.225 s. The transparency-supported condition also yielded higher usability ratings and lower perceived workload. These findings support TRACER as an inspectable workflow for CXR report review, verification-oriented consultation preparation, and prior-current comparison; clinical usefulness requires evaluation with patients and clinicians.

items.abstract: Lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) is a prevalent degenerative condition and a major cause of disability in aging populations. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred modality for assessment; however, severity grading remains inconsistent across readers and institutions, limiting reproducibility and complicating clinical decision-making. This study presents LSS-Net, a two-stage deep learning framework for automated grading of central canal stenosis using sagittal T2-weighted MRI. The first stage performs vertebral localization using a single-stage object detector, enabling standardized extraction of intervertebral regions of interest. The second stage applies a Swin Transformer-based classifier to predict stenosis severity (Normal/Mild, Moderate, Severe). The framework was developed using a multi-center dataset of 1,975 studies and evaluated on a held-out subset. Vertebral localization achieved 97.9% F1-score, while severity classification reached a weighted F1-score of 77.1%. Performance was highest for Normal/Mild and Severe classes, with reduced accuracy observed in Moderate cases, reflecting known diagnostic ambiguity. External clinical validation was conducted on an independent dataset using two expert readers. The model demonstrated substantial agreement with a neurosurgeon (accuracy 75.1%, κ=0.73 ) and moderate agreement with a neuroradiologist (accuracy 51.0%, κ=0.56 ), with inter-expert agreement in a comparable range. These findings suggest that LSS-Net may support more consistent and reproducible LSS grading. However, performance limitations in borderline cases and the restricted use of single-slice sagittal input highlight the need for further validation and extension to multi-sequence and multi-compartment analysis before clinical deployment.

items.abstract: 18F-FDG (18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose)-PET/computed tomography (CT) has emerged as a pivotal molecular imaging modality that extends beyond diagnosis to influence therapeutic decision-making in infectious and inflammatory diseases. By detecting increased glucose metabolism in activated inflammatory cells, it enables whole-body visualization of active disease before structural abnormalities become apparent on conventional imaging. Quantitative parameters support reproducible longitudinal monitoring. Its incorporation into international guidelines highlights its growing role in precision-guided management. Emerging technologies, including digital and long axial field-of-view PET/CT, artificial intelligence, radiomics, PET/MR imaging, and pathogen-specific or immune cell-specific tracers, may further enhance diagnostic accuracy and personalized treatment.

items.abstract: The nuclear entry of the capsid protein is a critical step in the life cycle of circoviruses, but whether capsid proteins from different circoviruses differ in their importin interactions remained unclear. Here, we modeled 298 unique circovirus capsid protein-importin pairs using AlphaFold 3. After conformational clustering and ZDOCK concordance filtering, 603 representative interfaces were retained for analysis. We extracted Δ iG values, interface features, and nuclear localization signal (NLS)-specific interface properties by PDBePISA and analyzed them with statistical tests. Capsid protein (Cap)-importin-9 (IPO9) complexes showed the lowest mean Δ iG among all tested circoviruses, identifying IPO9 as a candidate broadly interacting importin among the viruses examined. Across all host classes, Cap-importin β complexes showed a lower mean Δ iG than Cap-importin α or Cap-transportin complexes. Predicted Δ iG patterns differed across host classes, with distinct profiles for avian, mammalian, and fish circoviruses. Predicted Δ iG patterns and NLS interface features, including basic residue ratio, interface occupancy, and net charge, differed across avian, mammalian, and fish circoviruses. Together, these results provide a set of testable predictions regarding circovirus Cap-importin interfaces and highlight the predicted NLS interface as a region for further investigation.
