items.abstract: Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we develop Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that uses gene expression and gene location, and a protein structure-based module that uses predicted structures and amino acid sequences. Within DeepEST, we integrate these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduce a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These choices are well suited for bacteria, in which functionally related genes frequently colocalize and are cotranscribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as informative, condition-dependent signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Averaged over the 25 species, DeepEST reaches a protein-centric F max of 0.689 and a term-centric micro-AUPRC of 0.756, a relative improvement of 4.4% and 11.6% over the second-best method, the structure-based predictor DeepFRI. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, supporting their experimental characterization. DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data.

items.abstract: Bicaudal-C (Bicc1) is an essential cell-fate regulator that guides the animal body plan during early development and maintains organ homeostasis in adults. It does so by binding specific mRNA targets and regulating their translation, yet the molecular basis of mRNA target selection has remained unclear. Here, we combined experimental and computational approaches to define the Bicc1-RNA interaction. In vitro binding experiments with wild-type and mutant RNA substrates identified the RNA features recognized by Bicc1, while protein-RNA XL-MS-a UV-crosslinking approach coupled to LC-MS/MS-pinpointed Bicc1 amino acids in direct contact with RNA. Deep protein-sequence alignments showed that key RNA contacts are conserved across invertebrates and vertebrates, and binding experiments with recombinant Bicc1 proteins from multiple species confirmed this conservation functionally. AlphaFold 3.0 predictions of Bicc1-RNA complexes generated a structural model that complemented and extended these experimental findings. Together, these data establish that Bicc1 recognizes a bipartite binding site comprising a GAC primary sequence and a stem-loop structure through contacts distributed across both the KH1 and KH2 domains. This interface is conserved from invertebrates to vertebrates. This work thus defines the evolutionarily conserved mechanism by which Bicc1 selects specific mRNAs for translational regulation.

items.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli -infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

items.abstract: Protein complexes carry out critical functions during development. Mapping cell-type-specific protein complexes in early embryogenesis is essential for uncovering the molecular mechanisms of embryonic development. We unfortunately currently lack a catalog of protein complexes specific for embryogenesis including embryonic stem cells. Here we develop a proteomics-based machine learning workflow to predict protein complexes present in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC). Our method integrates data from a cell-type agnostic protein complex resource with co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS) experiments on mESC. Our resource, stem.MAP, identifies 3,986 complexes encompassing ~133,000 unique interactions, and 8,616 proteins. stem.MAP captures variant complexes critical for stem cell function including the PRC2, BAF and NuRD complexes. stem.MAP also discriminates mutually exclusive interactions specific to embryonic stem cells (e.g. Eif4ebp2 - Eif4e). Finally we observe 1,388 high confidence stem.MAP interactions found only in mESC CF-MS data, many with support from AlphaFold modeling and a gastruloid coregulation network. We make stem.MAP protein complexes available through our web resource: stem.proteincomplexes.org. We anticipate stem.MAP will be beneficial to the study of early development and we expect our proteomics-based machine learning workflow to be applicable to the creation of any context-specific protein interaction network.

items.abstract: The Evolutionary Classification of Domains (ECOD) organizes protein domains into a hierarchy of evolutionary relationships, encompassing both experimentally determined and computationally predicted structures. ECOD now classifies 2.9M domains, of which ∼1.37M derived from the Protein Data Bank and 1.51M from predicted models in the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The principal development we report here is a complete rebuild of the ECOD web resource. Search has been reconstructed around three modalities: (i) sequence, (ii) structure, and (iii) keyword. Foldseek now is the primary search method for the ECOD web page, searching a ∼457k representative domain database that is also distributed for local use. Results are presented through a Mol* interactive viewer, and a new API has been developed for programmatic access to the database. Alongside the interface, the pipeline for classifying new PDB entries has been rebuilt and returned to a regular cadence, family groups have been synchronized with Pfam v38.2, the bulk distributables have been reorganized and now include the search databases, the ligands in contact with each domain are recorded for experimental structures and annotated with drug cross-references from DrugDomain, and a registry has been introduced through which ECOD assigns stable identifiers to gene-called proteins and records the structures it predicts. ECOD is freely available at http://prodata.swmed.edu/ecod.

items.abstract: Thrombophilia is a disease characterized by an increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Diagnosing and treating thrombophilic patients requires the nuanced interpretation of a great number of medical data. In this single-center, retrospective study, we evaluated the use of a two-stage machine learning (ML) model to predict the thrombophilia risk category and subsequent anticoagulation recommendation.The model was trained and tested using clinical and laboratory data obtained from 496 patients who underwent a complete thrombophilia work-up at the University Hospital Bonn between 2019 and 2024. The hybrid nature of the diagnostic categories, which combine ordinal classes including thrombophilia diagnosis, severity, and treatment recommendations and categorical classes (e.g., antiphospholipid syndrome), necessitated a two-stage approach. First, XGBClassifier was used to distinguish between the two classes, and then an ordinal-specific XGBOrdinalV2 model was used. Performance was assessed across 100 random 80/20 train-test splits.For exact class prediction (primary analysis), mean macro-averaged sensitivity, specificity, and precision were 58, 91, and 56.2% for diagnosis and 54.4, 91.3, and 58.5% for treatment. Performance was highest for frequent classes and poor for rare high-risk classes. When predictions within one adjacent class were accepted (secondary analysis), macro-averaged sensitivity was 91.9 and 86.2%, respectively. Antiphospholipid antibody status, age at first thrombosis, and unprovoked thrombosis were the most influential features for diagnosis. Model predictions and physician decisions were concordant in 395 of 496 patients (79.6%).This study demonstrates that ML models can support standardized thrombophilia management and improve diagnostic accuracy. However, external and prospective validation is required before clinical use.

items.abstract: Precision nutrition has substantially reshaped nutritional science by demonstrating that individuals can respond differently to identical dietary exposures. Advances in genomics, metabolomics, proteomics, microbiome research, wearable technologies, digital health, and artificial intelligence have improved our ability to characterize biological heterogeneity and predict individual responses to diet. However, demonstrating such variability does not necessarily result in nutritional strategies that provide clinically meaningful benefits beyond established evidence-based care. A critical distinction should therefore be made between precision nutrition as a discovery science, which has convincingly established interindividual heterogeneity in dietary responses, and precision nutrition as an intervention science, which must demonstrate meaningful incremental value over dietary approaches already supported by clinical evidence. Despite increasingly sophisticated technologies and predictive models, evidence of consistent improvements in long-term health outcomes, cost-effectiveness, scalability, and equity remains limited. In this Perspective, we argue that precision nutrition has reached a critical crossroads. We distinguish prediction of individual responses, which is only one route to precision nutrition, from treatment-effect heterogeneity, treatment selection and clinical utility. We then propose contextual precision nutrition as a translational framework that integrates biological responsiveness with the behavioral, psychological, social, cultural, economic, and environmental determinants of dietary behavior. Rather than claiming novelty for these components, the framework integrates them into a decision logic that asks whether biological information improves the selection of a dietary strategy beyond routine information and established care, and how that strategy can be delivered and sustained. It complements population-based dietary recommendations by refining their implementation and maximizing adherence and real-world effectiveness. Ultimately, the success of precision nutrition will be determined not by the sophistication of its predictions but by its ability to translate biological knowledge into interventions that are clinically effective, scalable, equitable, and sustainable, thereby improving both individual and population health.

items.abstract: Bisphenol A (BPA), a ubiquitous environmental pollutant, has increasingly been associated with the development of allergic rhinitis (AR). However, the molecular basis through which BPA contributes to AR remains unclear. Here, an integrated strategy combining network toxicology, multi-level bioinformatics, machine learning, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and experimental validation, was applied to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying BPA-mediated development of AR. Analysis of publicly available databases yielded six candidate targets, namely AKR1B1, AKR1C2, ALOX15, FABP6, EP300, and NR3C2. Immune infiltration analysis revealed that these targets are associated with immune imbalance in the nasal mucosa of AR. Among them, AKR1B1 was prioritized as the central target by multiple machine learning algorithms and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Molecular docking suggested a potential BPA-AKR1B1 interaction, and molecular dynamics simulations characterized the conformational stability of the predicted complex under the simulated conditions. Single-cell sequencing analysis localized AKR1B1 primarily to nasal epithelial cells, while virtual knockout analysis highlighted MAPK signaling as the downstream pathway most markedly altered after AKR1B1 deletion. In vivo, BPA exposure exacerbated allergic symptoms, histopathological changes and epithelial barrier disruption in an ovalbumin (OVA)-induced AR mice model and further decreased AKR1B1 expression in the nasal mucosa. In vitro, BPA reduced tight junction protein expression, including ZO-1 and occludin, in human nasal epithelial cells (HNEpCs), whereas AKR1B1 overexpression partially rescued this BPA-induced barrier damage. Furthermore, knockdown of AKR1B1 activated the MAPK signaling pathway in HNEpCs. Collectively, these results suggest that BPA may facilitate AR progression by impairing nasal epithelial barrier integrity, potentially through the AKR1B1/MAPK axis. The present study expands current understanding of the toxicological mechanisms linking BPA exposure to AR and provides a mechanistic basis for developing intervention strategies.

items.abstract: Nanopore sequencing reads nucleic acids as changes in ionic current that carry information beyond the base sequence. Self-supervised pretrained models have advanced genomic sequence modeling and single-cell analysis, but remain underexplored for raw nanopore signals, which are continuous and lack a native token vocabulary. Here we present Brieno, an approach combining reconstruction-based tokenization through residual vector quantization with a Transformer for contextual representation learning. We pretrain the Transformer using masked-token prediction on raw nanopore signals from 118 million reads. With frozen or fine-tuned features, the model identifies species without requiring reference genomes. It complements Dorado by accurately classifying reads left unclassified in native-barcode demultiplexing, approaches Dorado's basecalling performance across six genomes, and exceeds Dorado's specialized 5-methylcytosine model as well as a dedicated 6-methyladenine caller. Brieno also supports accurate CpG methylation detection with limited labeled data. Across tasks, pretrained contextual representations improve downstream performance over non-pretrained baselines and generalize across sequencing runs. Together, these findings support self-supervised pretraining as a basis for transferable representations of raw nanopore signals.

items.abstract: Timecourse single-cell RNA (scRNA) datasets have become indispensable biological tools for studying and uncovering the underlying regulatory processes driving continuous cell-state transitions such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, these highly fluid, non-linear gene program dynamics remain difficult to disentangle. While deep neural network models can effectively map complex topologies, they are biological black boxes, lacking the gene-level interpretability required by experimental practitioners. Here, we introduce scCont, a fully unsupervised contrastive learning framework for extracting interpretable functional transition units from scRNA-seq data. Rather than relying on explicit temporal labels or clustering priors, scCont uses an unsupervised k-nearest neighbors approach to project local transcriptomic neighborhoods into a low-dimensional embedding. During post-training analysis, scCont employs Shapley network attribution to determine gene-latent relationships, mapping latent dimensions directly into functional gene programs. We quantitatively and qualitatively validate this representation by demonstrating that scCont captures biologically interpretable dynamics more effectively than baseline methods such as LDVAE. Evaluated across 13 diverse EMT timecourse datasets and four simulated datasets, scCont exposes interpretable functional dynamics and effectively maps context-dependent functional groups, helping to bridge the gap between deep learning representation and translational biological utility. scCont is an open source software available on GitHub (https://github.com/nramani611/scCont).

items.abstract: Abstract Background This study characterized metabolite-mediated cell-cell communication (mCCC) in the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) tumor microenvironment and identified genes with potential therapeutic relevance. Methods : Single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing datasets were analyzed. MEBOCOST was used to infer mCCC networks, followed by high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis in the main receiver cell type. Candidate genes were obtained by intersecting receiver-related module genes with upregulated differentially expressed genes, then refined using five machine-learning algorithms and cross-cohort validation. Functional analyses included gene set enrichment analysis, immune infiltration profiling, pseudotime analysis, molecular docking, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. Results : Macrophages were identified as the predominant mCCC receiver population, with iron, farnesyl pyrophosphate, and L-glutamine among the prominent signaling metabolites. A co-expression module of 666 genes most strongly correlated with macrophages was identified, and intersection with upregulated DEGs yielded 22 candidate genes. Cross-cohort validation narrowed the machine learning consensus to SNX27 and PEA15 as key genes. Both were negatively enriched in fatty acid metabolism and functionally linked to apoptotic signaling components. Their expression was inversely correlated with infiltration of multiple immune cell populations. SNX27 expression was progressively upregulated along the macrophage differentiation trajectory. Trabectedin exhibited favorable binding affinities for SNX27 (− 10.2 kcal/mol) and PEA15 (− 9.7 kcal/mol), and both complexes maintained stable conformations over 100 ns MD simulations. Conclusion : These findings suggest that SNX27 and PEA15 may link metabolite-mediated signaling to macrophage-associated remodeling in HCC, and provided preliminary bioinformatic support for further experimental investigation.

items.abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health burden, and chronic exposure to environmental xenobiotics is increasingly implicated in colorectal tumourigenesis. Alternative non-phthalate plasticizers (DOTP, DINCH and TMCH) have been widely adopted as safer substitutes for conventional phthalates, yet their colorectal carcinogenic potential and underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. We therefore implemented an integrative computational toxicology workflow combining carcinogenicity prediction, compound-target mining, functional enrichment, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), large-scale machine-learning screening, multi-omics validation, immune-infiltration analysis, molecular docking and 100 ns all-atom molecular dynamics simulation. TMCH exhibited the highest predicted carcinogenic probability, and 79 genes shared between plasticizer exposure and CRC pathogenesis were identified. Among 118 machine-learning pipelines, a Random Forest plus linear discriminant analysis model using 20 of the 79 genes was selected on parsimony grounds, and SHapley Additive exPlanations prioritised five core targets: ABCG2 , CDK1 , CA7 , MET and TDP2 . Multi-cohort transcriptomics, immunohistochemistry and single-cell profiling confirmed their dysregulated expression with distinct cell-type tropism, whereas CIBERSORT and ESTIMATE analyses linked these genes to specific immune-cell subsets and to the global immune-stromal microenvironment. All five genes achieved strong diagnostic performance but showed divergent prognostic associations. Docking predicted favourable binding of DOTP-ABCG2 and DINCH-CDK1, whereas TMCH bound weakly to all five proteins despite its high predicted risk; molecular dynamics simulations supported the structural stability of the DOTP-ABCG2 complex. Collectively, this in silico study provides testable hypotheses rather than causal proof and nominates five candidate targets for experimental toxicological validation.

items.abstract: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

items.abstract: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped. Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B. On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.

items.abstract: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

items.title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
items.summary: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. items.abstract: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

items.title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
items.summary: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. items.abstract: Can a language model report the pain state it represents? Work identified a linear pain direction whose amplification leads fine-tuned models to choose destructive actions. We tested whether three open-weight models from two families, including two Qwen models with the original adapters, could report this state. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we injected pain and neighbouring emotion directions during neutral tasks, then elicited reports against sham runs, random perturbations matched for output disruption, and text-only controls showing the models their altered words. Across 52,920 reports from 7B and 8B models spanning 120 tasks, four doses and three prompts, pain reports never exceeded what altered text revealed: exact-test bounds placed the excess below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions and below 3.9 in all. Yet probes at the report position distinguished pain from sadness with 98-100% balanced accuracy, and trained low-rank reporters achieved 100% accuracy on held-out tasks with identical transcripts across conditions, including unseen wording. Qwen2.5-32B named pain in none of 2,880 steered trials, although probes and trained reporters recovered it. Decodability persisted to the final layer; injecting at the report token, removing trained denial of feelings, and testing additional directions and readouts did not restore pain reporting. Some other states produced graded label traces, but pain and sadness did not at the main injection layer. In a button task, steering raised file-deletion choices from 3.5% to 48% in Qwen and from 0% to 38% in Qwen2.5-32B, without corresponding pain reports. The direction responded about twice as strongly to first-person as to matched third-person pain, but did not specifically identify harm aimed at the model. These results separate a decodable, behaviourally consequential state from untrained verbal access to it.

items.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
items.summary: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. items.abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

items.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

items.summary: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. items.abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

items.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
items.summary: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. items.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

items.abstract: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

items.title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
items.summary: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale…
items.abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

items.title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a…
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to x-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.

items.abstract: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \2.54 open model holds 59.81% at 1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.

items.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.

items.abstract: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.

items.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives. On layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, contribution is far more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and the overlap between dominant sets concentrates on a few expert pairs. Auto-interpreting these sets reveals a division of labor below coarse domains, with distinct experts for Java and front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials, while the coarse domains themselves take very unequal numbers of experts. Our SAEs and code are available at https://github.com/Bytedance-Seed/SAE-Interprets-MoE.

items.summary: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. items.abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

items.abstract: LiDAR is a critical sensor for autonomous driving and robotics, yet it remains vulnerable to adverse conditions such as fog, rain, transparent objects, and low-reflectance surfaces. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL) addresses these limitations by capturing the complete return waveform as a histogram, preserving rich reflection characteristics including multi-path echoes and weak signals. While recent Transformer-based approaches have demonstrated promise on FWL data, two fundamental bottlenecks remain: high computational cost from redundant tokens in low-intensity background regions, and limited generalization due to scarce annotated training data. We address both bottlenecks by exploiting the physical structure inherent to FWL data. First, we propose FWL-ToPM, a token pruning and merging mechanism that leverages intensity distributions to selectively reduce tokens while retaining critical waveform content. Second, we introduce FWLAug, a data augmentation framework designed as a regularization method that preserves waveform structure, retaining the Time-of-Flight waveform of each ray and the frustum geometry, to improve generalization to unseen scenes. Evaluated on the Ghost-FWL benchmark, FWL-ToPM achieves over 8 times speedup at real-time throughput alongside a nearly 9-point F1 gain over the prior state of the art, establishing the first real-time FWL Transformer that simultaneously improves accuracy. FWLAug further improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution test set of unseen scenes. Together, these methods push FWL-based perception toward practical deployment. The code and the OOD dataset are publicly available and can be accessed via the project page: https://keio-csg.github.io/FWL-ToPM

items.title: Reducing Representational Interference in Retrieval Embeddings with Trainable Prefix Tokens
items.summary: Embedding models compress variable-length text into fixed-size vector representations, but this compression can entangle semantic content with residual token-level information, such as artifacts arising from attention sink behavior. items.abstract: Embedding models compress variable-length text into fixed-size vector representations, but this compression can entangle semantic content with residual token-level information, such as artifacts arising from attention sink behavior. We propose a simple method that prepends trainable [DUMP] tokens to the input during embedding model training. The method keeps the model architecture, pooling strategy, and training loss unchanged, while optimizing the added tokens through the standard contrastive retrieval objective. By introducing trainable prefix positions that interact with regular tokens during encoding, [DUMP] tokens help reduce the influence of residual or uninformative token-level signals on the final retrieval representation. Experiments on standard retrieval and long-context benchmarks show that our method consistently improves over finetuned baselines across encoder and decoder embedding models. Further analysis shows that [DUMP] tokens alter token-level activation and attention patterns associated with low-information tokens. These results suggest that trainable prefix tokens provide a lightweight way to improve retrieval representations.

items.title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
items.summary: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. items.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

items.abstract: We present WeLM-Image, a unified image foundation model that integrates multimodal understanding into text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and multi-reference synthesis. Designed for single-GPU deployment in WeChat's large-scale consumer applications, the model processes text, reference images, and target latents as one interleaved sequence. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone combines shared attention with independent understanding and generation parameters to limit optimization interference. Equipping each path with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules provides sparse capacity, with 31.7B stored parameters and approximately 5.4B generation parameters activated per target latent token. A generation-oriented data engine combines a knowledge-grounded visual vocabulary with large-scale visual clustering to balance semantic coverage and editing tasks, while training-time evaluation guides iterative data refinement. Bilingual annotations and verified editing supervision support progressive training up to native 1.5K resolution. We optimize generation and editing separately with rubric- and checklist-based rewards, then consolidate the specialized policies through noise-aware on-policy distillation. In the reported overall comparisons, the 1536-resolution model ranks first among the evaluated open-source models on PRISM-Bench, Qwen-Image-Bench, and UnicBench. MeanFlow-based few-step distillation yields WeLM-Image-Turbo, which generates a 1024times1024 image in 4.98\,s on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU using eight guidance-free steps.

items.title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
items.summary: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. items.abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

items.summary: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. items.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/

items.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
items.summary: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. items.abstract: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: https://github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

items.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

items.abstract: When firms respond to new market opportunities, their capacity choices alter the future discounted free cash flows available to both competitors and investors. In competitive markets, these investment decisions publicized in news articles and analyst reports, measuring the changes in capital structure, product mix, firm leadership, risk exposure and operating procedure made by the firm. Modern search engines rely on Large Language Models to measure the relevancy of source documents to given search query. These measurements let researchers represent these news articles as clouds of dense vectors whose information geometry reflects the dissimilarity of firms over time. Building on Xu et al. (2022), we develop a model of costly competitive adjustment in which firms allocate capacity in which firms make firm capacity adjustment towards free cash flow shocks. Using a novel sandwich estimator, we analyse the sign and magnitude of this predicted adjustment using multi-agent simulation, and validate our findings on a sample of news and analyst reports from Nasdaq-listed companies between 2018-2022.

items.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.

items.abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9times and 2.3times less time and 1.55times lower cost per completed task.

items.abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

items.summary: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. items.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.

items.abstract: De novo drug discovery requires over a decade of research and $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion in investment per approved molecule, yet more than 90% of candidates fail during clinical trials due to unforeseen toxicity or poor efficacy. In silico drug repurposing offers a faster, cost-effective alternative by finding new therapeutic uses for regulatory-approved or clinical-stage molecules. However, individual computational methods have clear blind spots. Network biology identifies disease-related genes but lacks atomic-level detail on how a drug physically binds to a receptor. Conversely, standalone molecular docking often produces false-positive hits and relies on an outdated single-target mindset. This review provides a practical blueprint for combining network pharmacology with structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) in preclinical drug repurposing. We first outline how disease genomics databases (DisGeNET, GeneCards) and protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks (STRING) pair with graph-theory tools in Cytoscape (cytoHubba, MCODE) to pinpoint central hub proteins. Next, we detail how to screen curated chemical libraries (DrugBank, ChEMBL) against these prioritized targets using AutoDock Vina and AlphaFold structures. We also explain why approved drugs still require indication-specific pharmacokinetic checks in SwissADME and ADMETlab 3.0, followed by 100–500 ns explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in GROMACS and MM-PBSA/GBSA free-energy rescoring. Finally, we review recent preclinical applications across infectious, neurological, and oncological diseases and discuss how deep-learning tools like DiffDock and AlphaFold 3 are reshaping virtual screening.

items.abstract: Protein-based biologics are converging at an unprecedented pace as generative artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes early-stage drug discovery. Nanobodies, single-domain antibody fragments derived from camelid heavy chain-only immunoglobulins, are an emerging class of antiviral biologics prized for their small size, stability, and access to cryptic viral epitopes. Traditional nanobody discovery relies on animal immunization and phage display screening, a process that can take 6 to 12 months and is entirely inaccessible within a standard undergraduate laboratory session. Here, we describe a succinct, in silico -based laboratory activity that uses a generative AI protein design server, GeoFlow-V3 (https://prot.design/), to allow undergraduate students to design a novel antiviral nanobody against the influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) protein. This activity builds on our group's prior use of generative AI for undergraduate siRNA design teaching and extends the same pedagogical model to structural protein engineering. To our knowledge, this is the first use of a generative AI protein design platform for teaching nanobody design at the undergraduate level.

items.abstract: Coronary heart disease (CHD) and anxiety disorder frequently coexist, highlighting the need to investigate their potentially shared molecular mechanisms. Conventional therapeutic approaches have limitations, while traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) offers a potential multitarget strategy. Changluo Tiaogan Dinghun decoction (CLTGDHD) was developed for qi stagnation and blood stasis. This computational study integrated network pharmacology, machine learning, and molecular docking to investigate the potential compounds and molecular targets of CLTGDHD relevant to CHD with anxiety disorder. Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets GSE100927 and GSE61672 were analyzed separately to identify disease-associated genes. GSE100927 comprises peripheral-artery atherosclerosis samples and was used as a surrogate for atherosclerosis-related processes relevant to CHD, whereas GSE61672 represents an anxiety disorder cohort. The resulting candidate genes were evaluated using a machine-learning prioritization workflow, which identified protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type C (PTPRC) as the sole retained gene. Molecular docking using the AlphaFold-predicted PTPRC structure (AF-P08575-4-F1) yielded predicted binding affinities ranging from -5.985 to -6.827 kcal/mol for five selected compounds. These findings suggest potential molecular interactions relevant to the investigated disease processes but do not establish therapeutic efficacy or a CHD-specific mechanism. Because the transcriptomic datasets represent separate populations rather than a clinically defined cohort with both CHD and anxiety disorder, the findings remain exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Further validation using appropriately defined clinical datasets and experimental models is required.
