However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped…
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.

items.title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers
items.summary: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that…
items.abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.

items.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
items.summary: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but…
items.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

items.title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. items.abstract: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4-8-step regime down to just 1-2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

items.abstract: Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: https://svlwoof.github.io/gaussianrenderformer

items.abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

items.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus 5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs 107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \117 for teleoperation in China and below 290 in labour alone in North America.

By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. items.abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose LoopVQ, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to 4.3times and 6.1times on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

items.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
items.summary: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. items.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

items.title: Koopman Generative Operators for Efficient Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
items.summary: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and…
items.abstract: Probabilistic time-series forecasting requires models that simultaneously capture structured temporal dynamics, expressive uncertainty, and efficient inference, yet existing approaches fall short of this goal: latent dynamical models impose structure but rely on restrictive generation mechanisms, while modern generative methods such as diffusion and flow matching achieve flexibility at the cost of iterative and computationally expensive sampling. We introduce the Koopman Generative Operator (KGO), a probabilistic forecasting method that conceptualizes prediction as the evolution of structured uncertainty. KGO integrates three core components: (1) Koopman Patch Embedding (KoPE) for temporally consistent latent trajectory extrapolation; (2) Koopman Flow Matching (KoFM), which enables fast, single-step generation through a closed-form matrix exponential in a Koopman latent space, bypassing iterative sampling; and (3) an Adaptive Uncertainty Gate (AUG), which provides probabilistic forecasts by adapting uncertainty per-variable and per-horizon, corresponding to a learned decomposition of aleatoric uncertainty without manual tuning. By unifying these components, KGO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 13/17 ProbTS benchmarks in CRPS and 16/17 in NMAE. Further, by eliminating iterative sampling, KGO delivers at least a 25times reduction in inference time compared to iterative generative models. These results position KGO as a practical and principled framework that advances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in probabilistic time-series forecasting, combining leading accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks with fast, single-step generation.

items.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

items.abstract: A frontier AI model is trained in an AI data center, on tens of thousands of accelerators joined by a dedicated network, and every training step ends with all of them exchanging data at once. Between racks, that network is optical, and each of its four layers, from lasers to switches, runs a fixed or after-the-fact policy. Lasers sharing an enclosure, cooling, and power can fail together. At a fixed spare ratio, correlated failure provably caps a pool's availability however large it grows. In this paper, we present a comprehensive predictive control plane framework, called Halley, that reads each resource's next state and acts before the failure occurs. It has four components, each carrying a formal guarantee: LightReserve that sizes the laser pool to provide a coverage bound, FoldFit that schedules the switch within 11/9 of the optimal, ThermaLead that holds a microring with one-step-ahead control, and TriageGuard that protects the highest-risk modules first. Halley gives each layer a predictive controller that defers to the deployed policy when unsure. Composed from simulations at that point, effective goodput, the share of ideal throughput kept, rises from 65.2\% to 76.5\% if a window that exhausts its spares is lost. If only the dark channels' bandwidth is lost, it reaches 67.4\%. Per megawatt, that is up to 1.03--1.17 times the training; for the same training, up to 3.3--14.7\% less data center capacity. Halley's fallback circuits are formally verified and are shown to achieve close timing on a commercial FPGA, and pass a 130~nm signoff.

items.title: YANAMI: A Large-Scale Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Multiturn Stateful Interaction
items.summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) integrate visual understanding, generation, and editing within a single unified framework. However, existing unified multimodal datasets and benchmarks remain dominated by single-turn tasks. Even in recent multi-turn datasets, many turns can be solved independently without tracking information across turns. Consequently, they provide limited supervision and evaluation for multimodal…
items.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) integrate visual understanding, generation, and editing within a single unified framework. However, existing unified multimodal datasets and benchmarks remain dominated by single-turn tasks. Even in recent multi-turn datasets, many turns can be solved independently without tracking information across turns. Consequently, they provide limited supervision and evaluation for multimodal stateful interaction, which requires models to understand, maintain, update, and faithfully realize evolving dialogue states across turns. To address this gap, we introduce YANAMI, the first large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset and benchmark for stateful interaction, comprising YANAMI-400K and YANAMI-Bench. YANAMI-400K contains 400K multi-turn multimodal dialogues, with more than 2M images and 2.6M dialogue turns. The dialogues span four representative scenarios: Multi-Image Fusion, Image Editing, World Modeling, and Visual Reasoning, and require models to continuously track, preserve, and revise evolving multimodal dialogue states across turns. YANAMI-Bench comprises 400 multi-turn dialogues for systematically evaluating multimodal stateful interaction. It jointly evaluates Dialogue State Understanding and Visual Realization, characterizing the gap between models' ability to understand evolving dialogue states and their ability to faithfully realize them in visual outputs. Experiments show that fine-tuning BAGEL on YANAMI-400K improves image editing, generation, and multimodal stateful interaction by 10.3%, 2.0%, and 13.23%, respectively, while preserving its general visual understanding capabilities. Evaluations on YANAMI-Bench further reveal that existing UMMs still struggle to maintain, update, and visually realize evolving multimodal dialogue states.

items.title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems

items.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities. Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system. At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost? In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model and policy routing across general-purpose AI systems. We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality--cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance. To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct an omni-modal trajectory matrix spanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations. Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modal model routing, the capabilities of learned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency. Our results reveal substantial opportunities for capability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers outperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by 8.82x on average compared with the reference model.

items.title: Is Forgetting Unified? Exploring Concept Unlearning in Unified Multimodal Models
items.summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) integrate image generation and visual understanding, but are existing single-pathway unlearning methods sufficient to suppress target concepts across both? In this work, we study cross-pathway concept unlearning. Our goal is to prevent a model from both generating images of a target concept and identifying it in input images, while preserving other capabilities. To this end, we…
items.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) integrate image generation and visual understanding, but are existing single-pathway unlearning methods sufficient to suppress target concepts across both? In this work, we study cross-pathway concept unlearning. Our goal is to prevent a model from both generating images of a target concept and identifying it in input images, while preserving other capabilities. To this end, we introduce UUBench, a diagnostic benchmark covering 30 target concepts and 60 semantically related neighboring concepts. Experiments on representative UMMs show that the evaluated single-pathway methods achieve limited joint forgetting: generation-side editors strongly suppress target generation but yield limited forgetting in visual understanding, while understanding-side baselines struggle to achieve substantial forgetting even in their own pathway. Their direct composition also yields limited joint forgetting. We therefore propose UniForget, achieving joint forgetting rates of 80.0% on BAGEL-7B-MoT and 92.7% on Janus-Pro-7B, outperforming representative baselines. Further analysis reveals trade-offs between joint forgetting and capability preservation.

items.title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
items.summary: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire…
items.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

items.abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below 10^{-6}, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to 10^3 per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds 1.84 times 10^{19}, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor (SiLU(z) + δ, δin [0.01, 0.1]) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.

items.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
items.summary: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video…
items.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

items.title: From structure prediction to ligand-target recognition: expanding the reach of AlphaFold in natural product research.
items.summary: Natural products constitute a structurally diverse reservoir of bioactive molecules and remain an important source of lead compounds for drug discovery. items.abstract: Natural products constitute a structurally diverse reservoir of bioactive molecules and remain an important source of lead compounds for drug discovery. However, the limited availability of structural information on pharmacological targets and biomolecular interactions continues to hinder mechanism elucidation and structure-guided optimization, particularly for complex natural products such as bioactive peptides, proteinaceous natural products, and natural molecular glues. Recent advances in AlphaFold have transformed structural biology by enabling high-confidence prediction of protein structures and biomolecular complexes, providing unprecedented opportunities for structure-guided natural product research. Beyond conventional structure-based virtual screening, emerging co-folding strategies have demonstrated considerable potential for improving early enrichment in natural product screening and for elucidating the binding mechanisms of complex natural products with their targets. This review summarizes recent advances in AlphaFold-assisted natural product research, including target structure prediction, hit and lead discovery, co-folding-enabled interaction analysis, mechanistic investigation of peptide- and protein-derived natural products, and the emerging potential of AlphaFold for natural molecular glue discovery. We further discuss current limitations and future directions in structure prediction and interaction modeling. Overall, AlphaFold is reshaping natural product research from lead discovery to mechanistic characterization, with particular promise for advancing macromolecular natural products and molecular glue-mediated therapeutics.

items.abstract: Recent advances in protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction frameworks have the potential to accelerate computational drug discovery. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond their training sets. Mutation-dependent drug responses present a challenge to these methods because there are often large effects from relatively small perturbations. Here, we systematically benchmark diverse mutational effect and drug-target affinity prediction models using deep mutational scanning datasets spanning 11 inhibitor conditions for the MET kinase domain. Across both mutational effect prediction and drug–target affinity tasks, current AI models produce largely ligand-invariant predictions despite experimentally distinct inhibitor-dependent fitness landscapes. Ligand-aware geometric models, including LigandMPNN and LASErMPNN, partially recover experimentally validated resistance-associated hotspots, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling protein–ligand interactions and local structural flexibility. In contrast, deep learning affinity prediction models underestimate mutation-induced changes in binding affinity. This deficiency likely reflects mutation-invariant structural priors derived from co-folded structure prediction frameworks and the absence of mutation-conditioned supervision in current affinity datasets. Finally, we further extended our analysis to several kinase-inhibitor deep mutational scanning datasets and confirm the overall trends. Our findings suggest that a primary limitation in improving performance on this task lies in the scarcity of mutation-conditioned protein-ligand training data rather than model architecture alone.

items.abstract: Gemcitabine resistance remains a major therapeutic barrier in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), for which median survival in advanced disease has remained near one year despite extensive clinical investigation. Using artificial intelligence (AI)-guided structure-based drug repurposing, we identified sitagliptin, a DPP-4 inhibitor for diabetes, as a candidate ribonucleotide reductase (RRM1/2) inhibitor that sensitizes PDAC to gemcitabine. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that sitagliptin disrupts gemcitabine-RRM1/2 interactions, downregulating RRM1/2 expression and restoring chemosensitivity across PDAC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and mouse models. Sitagliptin enhanced the anti-tumor efficacy of both gemcitabine-nab-paclitaxel (GnP) and FOLFIRINOX regimens in preclinical studies. We conducted SITGEM-CARE, a single-center phase 2 trial in 22 patients with locally advanced or metastatic PDAC (median age 65.0 years; ECOG performance status 1, 86.4%; Stage IV, 68.2%; liver metastases, 54.5%). Patients received sitagliptin 100 mg orally once daily continuously, plus gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² and nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m² on days 1 and 8 of 21-day cycles. Among 22 evaluable patients, eight achieved a partial response, and 11 had stable disease, yielding an objective response rate of 36.4% (95% CI: 17.2-59.3%) and a disease control rate of 86.4% (95% CI: 65.1-97.1%), with tumor shrinkage in 86.4% of patients. At a median follow-up of 9.9 months, the median progression-free survival was 6.6 months (95% CI: 4.8-12.4) with 6-month and 9-month PFS rates of 63.6% and 43.5%, respectively. Median overall survival was 12.5 months (95% CI: 7.8-not reached), with 62.9% of patients alive at 12 months. Furthermore, treatment was well tolerated, with no Grade 4/5 treatment-related adverse events. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in adequately powered, randomized trials. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05947825.

items.abstract: Autoantibodies against type I IFNs can severely compromise antiviral defense, yet the mechanisms underlying their development remain elusive. Using high-throughput autoantigen profiling, we observed that a subgroup of severe COVID-19 patients exhibited strong binding to multiple type I IFNs. Integrated single-cell RNA and B cell receptor (BCR) sequencing with functional analysis identified B cell subsets/states enriched for IFN-α2-binding and -neutralizing antibodies in COVID-19. These findings were compared with those from patients with autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I, a rare genetic disease characterized by defective immune tolerance and persistent type I IFN autoimmunity. Competition surface plasmon resonance and AlphaFold 3 structural modeling identified three major functional epitope groups and seven predicted structural subclasses among neutralizing antibodies. Our results indicate that IFN-α2 autoreactivity is present in both naive and antigen-experienced B cell compartments, whereas functional IFN-neutralizing antibodies are predominantly associated with memory and atypical B cells, consistent with defective tolerance and affinity maturation-mediated selection of autoreactive B cell clones.

items.abstract: From protein structure prediction to novel protein generation, challenging protein engineering tasks have been made possible by advancements in machine learning (ML). While largely driven by ML architecture refinements, these advancements in ML-based protein engineering campaigns have left the impact of data curation underexplored. In light of the growing wealth of labeled sequence data, data-centric advances (e.g. prioritizing improvements in ML protein engineering tools through the curation of high-quality, domain-specific training data) are increasingly preferred over model-centric advancements. Implementing datasets that accurately reflect biological complexity and diversity has been shown to improve the efficiency of training protein engineering ML tools. Here, we evaluate an ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)-informed data augmentation strategy for training generative and representation-learning models in protein engineering. Using ethylene-forming enzyme (EFE) as a model system, we show that variational autoencoder models trained on ancestral and near-ancestral sequence datasets generate variants with improved predicted and experimentally measured thermostability relative to variants generated from modern-sequence training data. All experimentally tested ancestral and ML-generated EFEs produced detectable ethylene, although ML-generated variants showed reduced activity relative to wild-type EFE, indicating that the approach more strongly captured stability-associated features than catalytic optimization. We further evaluated ASR-enriched sequence sets for fine-tuning ESM2 representations in endolysin and lysozyme C stability-classification tasks, where ancestral representations were competitive with modern-sequence fine-tuning in selected settings. Overall, this work supports ASR-informed data augmentation as a promising strategy for stability-oriented protein sequence generation and motivates future work to couple ancestral sequence diversity with explicit functional selection.

items.summary: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling ( ipTM ) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors ( PAEs ) between molecular tokens. items.abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling ( ipTM ) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors ( PAEs ) between molecular tokens. These errors are directional: the predicted position of tokens in one molecule is evaluated relative to coordinate frames defined by tokens in another. The PAE matrix is therefore asymmetric, but AF3 reports the maximum of the two directional pairwise ipTM scores, whereas Boltz-2 reports them separately. In both programs, the TM-score scaling parameter, d 0 , depends on molecular system size rather than solely on the component being scored. In protein–protein complexes, including disordered regions and domains unrelated to the interface can further lower ipTM . I previously introduced the interaction predicted score from aligned errors ( ipSAE ) to address these limitations for protein–protein complexes. Here, I extend ipSAE to interactions involving proteins, nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, and atomic ions. The framework makes three explicit choices for each molecular pair: which component supplies the alignment frames, which tokens are scored, and how d 0 is defined. For different molecular types, I propose aligning on the more complex molecule and scoring the simpler one. For protein–ligand complexes, this entails aligning on protein residues, scoring all ligand heavy atoms without a PAE cutoff, and using a fixed d 0 of 2 Å. In benchmarks of 102 protein–ligand complexes predicted by AF3 and Boltz-2, this formulation yields a substantially wider range of confidence scores than native ipTM . On a held-out set of 82 complexes, thresholds of 0.5 for AF3 and 0.8 for Boltz-2 classified ligand placements with balanced accuracies of 0.938 and 0.862, respectively, using a ligand RMSD threshold of 5 Å. Protein–DNA benchmarks support the same directional scoring scheme, while smaller protein–RNA benchmarks provide a preliminary assessment. These results establish a framework for interpreting predicted structural confidence across different classes of biomolecular interactions and suggest that directional scoring may also be useful for computationally designed protein binders. The Latin phrase “Rēs ipsae adhūc loquuntur” in the title means “The things themselves are still speaking” referring to the PAE scores and what they tell us about protein/ligand and protein/nucleic acid interactions in cofolding models. The new IPSAE code is freely available from: https://github.com/DunbrackLab/IPSAE2 .

items.abstract: Cytoplasmic dynein transports diverse cargoes toward microtubule minus ends following activation by the dynactin complex and cargo adapters. In elongated cells such as fungal hyphae and neurons, dynein must first undergo kinesin-1-dependent transport to microtubule plus ends to engage cargoes, but the mechanism linking these opposing motors remains poorly understood. Here, we identify KobA in the filamentous fungus Aspergillus nidulans as a kinesin-1-binding, coiled-coil protein essential for kinesin-1 (KinA)-mediated plus-end transport of dynein and dynactin. KobA binds the C-terminal cargo-binding domain of KinA. Interestingly, KobA is not required for the general function of KinA in supporting hyphal growth alongside myosin-V, but is specifically required for the microtubule plus-end accumulation of dynein-dynactin even when KinA is activated. Mechanistically, KobA enhances the interaction between KinA and dynactin-dynein. Within its disordered N-terminal region, KobA harbors a Spindly motif typically present in dynein-activating cargo adapters that engage the dynactin pointed end. AlphaFold-3 predictions suggest that the Spindly motif of KobA also binds the dynactin pointed end, and in support of this notion, point mutations within the KobA Spindly motif disrupt the KinA–dynactin association, causing dynein to decorate microtubules rather than accumulate at plus ends. Together, our findings establish KobA as a novel adapter that utilizes a classic cargo adapter Spindly motif to link kinesin-1 to dynein-dynactin, ensuring targeted plus-end delivery of the minus-end motor.

items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) carriage is associated with poor outcomes in patients with liver cirrhosis, which is worsened by repeated antibiotic exposure and hospitalizations. While the semi-synthetic rifamycin derivative, rifaximin, has recently been linked to ARG expansion preclinically, the effects of rifamycin SV MMX (RiVM) on the gut resistome remain unknown. We evaluated longitudinal resistome changes with RiVM in cirrhosis. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled RIVET trial (15 RiVM, 15 placebo) included compensated cirrhosis patients who underwent shotgun metagenomic sequencing before/after 30 days of therapy. ARGs were annotated using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database. The longitudinal resistome was evaluated using univariable and multi-variable methods (LEfSe, paired-Wilcoxon testing, and MaAsLin3), and machine learning (ML) was used to determine ARG changes at subject and group levels. RiVM induced minimal perturbation of the gut resistome, without significant change in ARGs versus after FDR adjustment. Complementary approaches (univariable and multivariable) identified a trend towards lower vancomycin resistance ARGs, including vanW and vanT operon-associated genes, after RiVM exposure. In contrast, several Enterobacteriaceae-associated multidrug efflux regulators (including evgS, emrK, and mdtA) showed nominal increases post-rifamycin that did not withstand FDR. Group-level ML demonstrated limited discrimination between groups; however, within-subject longitudinal models achieved improved classification performance. No increase in infections or treatment-related safety concerns was observed. We conclude that rifamycin MMX was not associated with infections and did not enrich antimicrobial resistance genes compared to placebo in a small randomized 30-day clinical trial in patients with compensated cirrhosis. There was a tendency towards reduced vancomycin resistance and ARG reduction after rifamycin exposure. Registration: NCT04082780 www.clinicaltrials.gov.

items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including medical chatbots, are increasingly integrated into health care delivery. While prior research emphasizes diagnostic accuracy and usability, less is known about the psychological and contextual factors that shape patients' trust and preferences for AI versus human providers, particularly among patients who have experienced medical stigma. Purpose This study investigates when and why patients may prefer medical chatbots over human providers, focusing on the roles of prior experiences of stigma, comfort with medical AI, and the contextual tradeoff of wait time. Methodology/approach Two scenario-based experiments examined trust in a chatbot versus a human provider (N=300) and choice between a chatbot and a human provider depending on wait time (N=450). Measures included trust in the provider (perceived accuracy and bias), past experiences of medical stigma, and comfort with medical AI. Results In general, participants preferred human providers. However, participants who reported high comfort with medical AI and those with prior experiences of stigma (e.g., related to weight, mental health, or gender identity) expressed greater trust in the chatbot. Moderation analysis confirmed significant interaction effects between provider type, comfort with medical AI, and stigma history. Conclusions Preferences for AI-driven care are conditional. Chatbots may offer psychological safety and perceived impartiality for patients with stigmatized identities. Practice implications Providers are often challenged with managing high caseloads and allocating appointments. Integrating chatbots in care pathways could improve access to care and enhance trust among marginalized populations, especially for low-stakes concerns, offering cost-effective, patient-centered alternatives in selected contexts.

items.abstract: Nutrition clinicians need to recognize the importance of establishing meaningful connections with their patients and family members. In this manuscript, we discuss skills for making these connections and possibly reducing the risk of nutrition-related ethical dilemmas. American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition leaders have stressed the importance of clinician-patient connections. Insights from Jonathan Rhoads, who was a developer of parenteral nutrition, indicated that availability and affability are important traits for nutrition clinicians, not just ability. These qualities reflect a patient-centered approach grounded in compassion, empathy, and effective communication. We present two examples of teaching tools designed to develop these skills in nutrition clinicians. (1) A nutrition clinician play performed at the ASPEN Clinical Nutrition Week 2015 that used spoken words and nonverbal communication to demonstrate approaches to connecting with a patient's family members. (2) A module developed for graduate nutrition students in 2025 that uses an artificial intelligence-generated role-play simulation to provide practice engaging in conversations with patients and caregivers involving crucial issues about the use of artificially administered nutrition and hydration.

items.abstract: Background Vascular geometry may impede catheter navigation during mechanical thrombectomy. We evaluated whether cervical curvature predicts recanalization success. Methods This is a retrospective single-center cohort of 160 anterior large vessel occlusion patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy at a comprehensive stroke center (Barnes-Jewish Hospital/Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO) from May 2019 to February 2021. Cervical curvature was computed using 3-dimensional vessel centerlines derived from preprocedural computed tomography angiography. Primary outcomes were successful recanalization (final modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction score ≥2b) and intracranial access time (puncture→first pass). Associations were evaluated with multivariable linear or logistic regression, adjusting for age, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, first-line device, and access route. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models with Gini Importance and Shapley Additive Explanation explained feature importance. Results Mean age was 67±15 years; median National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale 16; mean total curvature was 9.80±2.85. Median intracranial access time was 24 minutes (interquartile range, 17-32), with no correlation to cervical curvature (ρ=0.054; adjusted β=0.20 min/unit [95% CI, -0.75, 1.15]; P =0.676). Successful recanalization occurred in 86% and varied across curvature tertiles (low 91%, mid 93%, high 75%; P =0.017). Per-unit curvature increase was associated with recanalization failure (adjusted odds ratio, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.02-1.43]; P =0.028). Receiver operating characteristic-derived curvature threshold (>11.54) identified a high-risk group (adjusted odds ratio, 5.10 [95% CI, 1.88-13.84]; P =0.001). Machine learning confirmed cervical curvature as the dominant predictor, with a Shapley Additive Explanation peak effect at 11.65. Conclusions Cervical curvature independently predicts mechanical thrombectomy recanalization failure, with a threshold effect near 11.6 units. Preprocedural curvature assessment derived from routine computed tomography angiography may improve risk stratification and inform mechanical thrombectomy strategy.

items.abstract: Background Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a severe inflammatory lung injury caused by various factors, including infection, trauma and shock. The predominant pathological alteration in its late stages is pulmonary fibrosis (PF), characterised by progressive extracellular matrix deposition, architectural destruction and functional impairment. Particularly in COVID-19-induced ARDS, PF incidence has markedly increased, making it a major sequela impacting patients' long-term quality of life. Methods This review systematically examines post-acute lung injury (ALI)/ARDS PF through three perspectives: pathogenesis, prediction and treatment. Results Mechanistically, the fibrotic process involves epithelial injury and mesenchymal transition, fibroblast activation with aberrant extracellular matrix remodelling, dysregulated inflammation with immune cell involvement and clinical management-related factors. For prediction, various biomarkers (including growth factors, matrix proteins and inflammatory markers) and imaging features (particularly high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics) demonstrate clinical value. Integrated multiparameter models incorporating artificial intelligence show promise for early identification and risk stratification of high-risk patients. Therapeutic strategies encompass anti-inflammatory approaches (e.g., corticosteroids and antioxidants), antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone and nintedanib), cell-based therapies (mesenchymal stem cells and exosomes) and emerging genetic/RNA interventions. However, specific preventive and therapeutic approaches tailored to the post-ALI/ARDS PF population remain inadequate in clinical practice. Conclusions Future research should focus on elucidating underlying mechanisms, refining early-warning systems, exploring personalised treatments and facilitating clinical translation. The ultimate goal is to transition from traditional supportive care to proactive prevention through enhanced clinical surveillance, early prediction and rational intervention, thereby preventing fibrosis progression and improving outcomes in ARDS survivors.

items.abstract: Background Preoperative total body weight loss (PreopTBWL%) is widely used before metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS), yet its long-term prognostic value remains debated. This study integrated machine learning (ML), unsupervised clustering, and linear mixed-effects modeling (LMM) to define data-driven preoperative targets and characterize multi-year postoperative weight trajectories. Methods We analyzed prospectively collected data and electronic medical records from 802 adults undergoing primary laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, primary Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, or revision/conversion MBS within a structured, protein-focused preoperative lifestyle program. Five machine learning models were trained with nested cross-validation to predict each postoperative year. Each model used only patients with that year's outcome recorded (608 at Year 1 to 83 at Year 6). From Year 2 onward, earlier postoperative measurements for those patients were included as predictors. Priority was given to Years 1-4. Top-performing SHAP profiles guided feature selection for confirmatory longitudinal LMMs. Although the LMM framework spanned the full 6-year horizon (858 repeated measures from 420 active patients), the most robust inferences were restricted to Years 1-4 because of substantial attrition thereafter. Youden Index optimization, segmented regression, and unsupervised k-means clustering on UMAP embeddings were used to define precise PreopTBWL% targets and map distinct multi-year phenotypic subgroups. Results Machine learning models demonstrated strong predictive performance, peaking at Year 2 (Random Forest R² = 0.524 ± 0.033, AUC = 0.875 ± 0.029) and remaining robust through Year 4, with PreopTBWL% consistently ranking among the strongest prognostic features. Unsupervised clustering (k = 5) revealed that preoperative behavioral engagement separated high- from low-performing phenotypes far more powerfully than procedure type or demographics. Initial racial disparities in weight-loss trajectories narrowed progressively and were no longer statistically significant by Year 4 (p = 0.1454). Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed a robust, independent positive association between PreopTBWL% and long-term outcomes (β = 0.447, p < 0.001). Threshold optimization identified 10.5% PreopTBWL% as the optimal clinical target; patients falling below this threshold experienced a significant long-term deficit (β = -4.608, p = 0.017) that persisted after adjustment for diabetes and operative duration. Interaction terms between the threshold and surgical procedure were non-significant (Threshold × Sleeve, p = 0.532; Threshold × Revision/Conversion, p = 0.778). Segmented regression further identified a structural dose-response breakpoint at 19.68% PreopTBWL%. Conclusions Achieving ≥ 10.5% PreopTBWL% was associated with durable multi-year PostopTBWL% after MBS, and procedure type did not modify that association in this cohort. By integrating predictive machine learning with explanatory longitudinal modeling, this work shifts preoperative evaluation from arbitrary administrative requirements toward structured, phenotype-guided risk stratification and care escalation.

items.abstract: Purpose of review Digital devices play an increasingly important role in the detection and screening of cardiac arrhythmias. Atrial fibrillation (AF), the most common arrhythmia, is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. This review summarises the current evidence on wearable devices for screening and diagnosing atrial fibrillation. Recent findings Numerous studies have demonstrated the value of wearables for AF detection and diagnosis. In addition, artificial intelligence enhances automated rhythm analysis and signal processing, supporting the increasing clinical implementation of digital technologies in outpatient care. Single-lead ECG devices provide the strongest evidence for AF detection, with smartwatches representing one of the most extensively investigated wearable technology. Limitations include motion artefacts and predominantly semi-continuous monitoring. Future research should focus on integrating artificial intelligence to improve signal analysis and artefact reduction, and on evaluating the impact of wearable-based strategies on clinically relevant outcomes, including stroke and heart failure.

items.abstract: By hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome system to catalytically degrade pathogenic proteins, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) offers unprecedented opportunities to eliminate intractable targets, dismantle scaffolding functions, and achieve deeper, more durable therapeutic responses. This chapter provides a forward-looking examination of the field, moving beyond proof-of-concept to address the critical chemical, biological, and translational questions that will define the next decade. We dissect the evolution of degrader design, from expanding the ligand toolbox to target previously "undruggable" proteins, to engineering programmable degradation platforms with spatiotemporal and logic-gated control. A central focus is placed on the deep integration of artificial intelligence, which is reshaping rational design by predicting ternary complex dynamics and ubiquitin transfer efficiency. Crucially, we confront the translational conundrums head-on, analyzing the unique pharmacokinetic /pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) relationships, the multi-layered mechanisms of acquired resistance, and the dual nature of collateral degradation in the context of therapeutic safety. By bridging state-of-the-art medicinal chemistry with clinical pharmacology, we delineate a roadmap for harnessing this transformative modality to deliver on its promise for patients, particularly in oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration.

items.abstract: Triamcinolone acetonide (TA) is a widely used glucocorticoid for inflammatory diseases, including arthritis. Although intra-articular TA injection provides effective symptom relief, its safety profile in real-world clinical practice remains incompletely characterized. Adverse event reports associated with intra-articular TA injection for arthritis were retrieved from the FAERS database (2004-Q1 2026) and the JADER database (2004-Q4 2025). Disproportionality analyses were performed using four signal detection algorithms, including ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate signal heterogeneity and robustness. Time-to-onset patterns were assessed using Weibull analysis. Endocrine-related adverse events were further evaluated using multivariable logistic regression and machine learning classification models with SHAP-based interpretation. A total of 738 FAERS reports involving intra-articular TA were identified, covering 27 system organ classes. Multiple established and potential safety signals were detected, including adrenal insufficiency, hyperglycemia, osteonecrosis, bacterial arthritis, postmenopausal hemorrhage, and Cushing's syndrome. Additional potential safety signals included type 2 diabetes mellitus, flushing, erythema multiforme, pemphigus, and septic shock. The strongest disproportionality signals were observed for injection site calcification, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, injection site atrophy, and Cushing's syndrome. Most adverse events occurred within 30 days after exposure (84.55%), with a median onset time of 5 days (IQR: 2-14). External signal consistency assessment using 112 JADER reports identified eight signals consistent with FAERS findings. Multivariable logistic regression showed that age, sex, therapy type, and reporter type were associated with endocrine-related adverse event reporting. Machine learning models demonstrated good classification performance, with random forest achieving the highest test set AUC (0.864). SHAP analysis identified demographic and treatment-related variables as important contributors to model classification. This study provides a comprehensive real-world pharmacovigilance assessment of intra-articular TA and identifies both established and potential safety signals. Integration of conventional signal detection, regression analysis, and interpretable machine learning approaches may facilitate systematic characterization of TA-associated adverse event patterns and support future safety monitoring.

items.abstract: Background Despite rapid advances in computational pathology, including foundation-model embeddings, most approaches remain classifier-based. Breast lesion pathology is an area of unmet clinicopathological need and a compelling setting for morphology-based modeling: diagnostic categories occupy overlapping morphological spectra and reflect heterogeneous pathways of tumor development, thereby posing substantial challenges for pathological diagnosis and subsequent clinical decision-making. However, approaches to delineate morphological continua across diagnostic categories and tumor development remain understudied. Here, we leveraged morphology-based foundation-model embeddings to define a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories and dissect how these embeddings could reflect a pathobiological continuum or sequence associated with tumor development. Methods To model breast lesion categories in continuous morphology space, we established a leakage-controlled, patient-aware workflow using the frozen foundation model Prov-GigaPath and the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset, a pathologist-annotated hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) breast lesion dataset spanning normal tissue, benign proliferative lesions, atypical lesions, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive carcinoma (IC). Using the BRACS training split, we defined a train-derived principal component analysis (PCA) morphology space. We then performed two complementary analyses: normal-rooted k-nearest-neighbor (kNN)-Dijkstra graph-distance scoring to derive a trajectory-like morphology score without imposing the full ordinal diagnostic sequence; pairwise Energy distance and squared maximum mean discrepancy with a radial-basis-function kernel (RBF-MMD²) to quantify order-free distributional separation among diagnostic categories. Validation and test data were projected into the train-defined reference space to assess reproducibility. Results Prov-GigaPath embeddings defined a train-derived morphology space with category-associated organization. Without imposing the full diagnostic sequence, normal-rooted kNN-Dijkstra graph distances recovered a trajectory-like morphology arrangement from normal/benign to malignant lesions. Order-free Energy distance and RBF-MMD² further supported graded separation among lesion categories. Validation and test datasets preserved the pathological organization. Furthermore, morphological embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma, without requiring additional molecular information. Conclusions Leveraging morphology-based foundation-model embeddings, we defined a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories, allowing nuanced positioning of breast lesions along a pathobiological continuum associated with tumor development. Our approaches pave the way for extracting biologically and clinically relevant information from routine histopathology to guide molecular testing, individualized risk assessment, and cost-efficient clinicopathological decision-making. Highlights Overlapping morphological features challenge breast diagnostic categorization Foundation-model embeddings defined a morphologic state space Embeddings allow nuanced positioning along morphological continua across categories Embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma Latent morphological signals in H&E slides may refine individualized risk assessment

items.abstract: Background Estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2 status guide systemic treatment in breast cancer. Multimodal models are rarely benchmarked against key biomarker molecular baselines or evaluated for cross-cohort calibration. We assessed incremental value, dependence on label-proximal HER2 transcripts, and transport of discrimination and calibration. Methods A model combining whole-slide images, transcriptomes, age and stage was developed in TCGA-BRCA (1051 patients; ER/PR/HER2 analysis sets: 1001/998/1006) and evaluated in CPTAC-BRCA (120 patients; 118/113/95). CPTAC had been observed during earlier development and included 13 HER2-positive cases. Analyses included paired model comparisons, transcript removal, alternative loss functions and recalibration. Internal discrimination used pooled out-of-fold predictions; external discrimination used fold-mean estimates, with ensemble calibration reported separately. Internal calibration and macro-AUC uncertainty were interpreted as exploratory. Results Internal AUCs were 0.943 for ER, 0.901 for PR, and 0.860 for HER2; external AUCs were 0.952, 0.937, and 0.918, respectively. External macro-AUC was 0.936 for the multimodal model and 0.957 for logistic regression using ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 (difference −0.021). Removal of the extended 29-transcript 17q12–q21 region changed HER2 AUC by −0.035 [−0.058 to −0.013] (95% CI) internally and by −0.042 [−0.089 to −0.007] externally relative to the base-line multimodal model. For external 15-model ensemble predictions, recalibrated HER2 expected calibration error (ECE) was 0.236, exceeding the ECE reference ceiling of 0.125, while calibration-in-the-large was −1.657 [−2.373 to −1.023] (profile-likelihood 95% CI), indicating systematic overprediction. ER and PR also showed overprediction. In paired fold-mean comparisons, HER2 ECE and Brier score favoured the three-transcript model (ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2). Conclusions A multimodal deep-learning model achieved high discrimination across cohorts but did not demonstrate clear incremental value over a par-simonious three-transcript baseline, while cross-cohort calibration remained a substantial challenge. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating incremental value, calibration, and clinical utility alongside discrimination when assessing AI-based prediction models for medical use.

MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection. However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA). Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference. Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified. Across included studies, the bivariate meta-analysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 - 0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 - 0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I2 = 7.3%). In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809). For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p≥0.192). Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity. Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC. The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification. Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.

items.abstract: Background: Previous research has shown that clinical prediction models have likely been 'hacked' to meet arbitrary performance thresholds. However, this work only assessed abstracts, could not identify models with a perfect AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) of 1, and did not examine other performance metrics. Methods We collected data from full texts and validated a large language model to extract data from a random sample of Q1 journal articles for 2025. We examined if hacking occurred in the AUC value, sensitivity and specificity, and checked if articles correctly reported the AUC value from corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Results We identified 2,001 prediction model articles that reported 15,656 AUC values. We found a striking excess of results near perfect prediction and at multiples of five and ten for the AUC, sensitivity and specificity, indicating likely manipulated data, methods or publication bias. Around 1 in 40 AUC values were reported outside of their confidence intervals, and around 1 in 8 ROC curves did not match their reported AUC value. Conclusion We have shown that not only the AUC value, but the sensitivity and specificity are being hacked, likely to help the authors publish their paper at the cost of evidence for practice. Excess models that are not representative of their true performance may misguide clinicians, distort the literature, and make it harder to find prediction models that are useful for practice.

items.abstract: Advances in RNA sequencing have established transcriptomics as a key approach for investigating gene expression, regulation, and functional diversity across both model and non-model organisms. In the absence of high-quality reference genomes, de novo transcriptome assembly remains essential, yet its accuracy and reproducibility depend heavily on the choice and integration of computational strategies. This review provides a comprehensive and structured framework for de novo transcriptome reconstruction and functional annotation in non-model systems, integrating current best practices across quality control, assembly, redundancy reduction, and annotation workflows. We systematically compare short-read, long-read, and hybrid assembly approaches, and evaluate multi-layered annotation strategies combining homology-based, domain-based, and ontology-driven methods. We further highlight emerging developments, including long-read transcriptomics, machine learning-assisted annotation, orthology inference, and multi-omics integration, which improve transcriptome completeness and biological interpretability. Key limitations in current workflows are critically examined, including database biases, incomplete annotations, and challenges in isoform resolution, particularly in underrepresented taxa. By consolidating methodological advances with practical recommendations, this review proposes a reproducible and scalable roadmap for transcriptome analysis in non-model organisms. We also discuss future directions, including the development of inclusive reference databases, AI-driven annotation frameworks, and open, containerized infrastructures aligned with FAIR principles to support global transcriptomics research.

items.abstract: Motivation Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell’s own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. Results We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. Availability scSTEC is freely available at https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC .
